speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways) :
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I beg leave to introduce a bill to incorporate the Canadian Railway Express Company.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The object of this bill is to incorporate an express company for the purpose of enabling the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway to effect economies and to provide more remunerative operation with respect to their respective express services, pursuant to the provisions of Part II of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Railway Act, 1933, if, as and when the trustees and directors of the two railways respectively determine that this should be done.
The only reason I should like to have the privilege of introducing this bill to-day, and a similar bill with respect to telegraphs, is to afford many hon. members, who have asked for copies of the bills, an opportunity of seeing them. The bill, for leave to introduce which I am now asking, commits no one to anything; it is simply an enabling bill the purpose of which is to permit the companies, if finally they come to an agreement, to carry out this measure. They have not yet come to such agreement and there is no certainty that they will; but both railways, through Mr. Beatty and Mr. Fullerton respectively, have written to me asking me to introduce these two bills and to endeavour to have them adopted by the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can the minister advise the house as to why it is that this particular bill has been held until this time? Why was notice not given earlier in the session? The house has had no notice of the intention of the minister to introduce such a bill this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The government had no information in regard to the matter, because the railway companies did not request us until very recently to introduce these bills. Apparently they had not arrived at the position of discussing an agreement of this kind until quite recently, when they wrote to me, and naturally I preferred that they should submit the bills themselves. They could have done so except for want of time, and they have asked us to deal with the matter. There is also a bill with respect to telegraph service along exactly the same lines, and if I am permitted to introduce at the present time the bill with respect to the Canadian Railway Express Company I shall ask for leave to introduce the other.
Is this bill a first step towards the amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is not a step towards the amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. I shall explain the matter when it is before the house, but I may say that what is contemplated here is permitted under the act of last year with respect to subsidiary companies. It has nothing at all to do with the amalgamation of the railways; it deals entirely with the proposed express company in this case, and, in the other, with telegraphs.

policy should be a matter of government responsibility, and I do not see why the power of deciding monetary policies should be handed over to an institution which is not owned by the government. The time has arrived when cooperation between the institution that is going to determine the monetary policy of Canada and the government should be just as close as the cooperation between the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Finance. I can see no good reason why this institution should be set up under any but public ownership. I consider it a retrograde step at this time to establish a privately owned institution with the great powers conferred by this bill, and for that reason I support very heartily the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are three reasons
why the government is not prepared to accept this amendment. First, the experience of the world indicates that such a proposal would be bad. Second, it is essential that the bank should be free from political control. Third, all profits of the bank except $225,000 accrue to the people, to the country, and to all intents and purposes the bank itself is a publicly owned bank, for (a) the provisional directors are named in the bill, and (b) the governor, the deputy governor and the bylaws must be approved by the government of the day. In other words the operation of the bank must be subject to the approval of the government of the day, as to the personnel of its officers and the laws under which it operates.
Dealing very briefly with the matter-because it has been dealt with at such length that I do not propose to cover the ground again-I shall take the first point, namely, the question of the experience of the world. Central banks are either privately owned or bank owned, or partly privately and partly state owned. I think that is a fair way to put it. The countries in which the central banks are wholly owned by the public are, as I said in the committee, six in number, namely Australia, Bulgaria, Finland, Latvia, Russia and Sweden. The conditions under which the central bank of the Commonwealth of Australia became publicly owned were set out at length in the speech delivered by the Minister of Finance.
Those wholly privately owned are Albania, Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Danzig, Esthonia -the government owns a few shares, and is disposing of them-France, India, Germany, Hungaria, Italy, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland. In those countries the central banks are privately owned, without limitations such as are imposed here with respect to either returns to the shareholders, or the restricting and supervising power exercised over the institution by the government of the country. That does not apply to all. In some instances the supervision is much the same as it is here. The wholly bank owned central authority is. of course, found in the United States of America. Technically it is not probably correct to say that the reserve banks of the United States could be described as central banks, but the banks are members of the central reserve body and therefore own the central reserve banks in the various parts of the United States.
Those which are part publicly and part privately owned are found in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Greece-where there is a limitation upon the amount of stock which may be owned by the government-and in Japan, where the same provision prevails, Lithuania, and Rou-mania. In Czechoslovakia and Roumania there is a limitation in the extent to which stock may be held in the central bank.
Public, private and bank owned are found in Chile, Colombia, and Peru. And there is private and bank ownership in South Africa. That is the position as indicated by the experience of the world. While, as I said the other day, it is not always desirable to rely upon the experience of other countries in arriving at conclusions in your own country- because conditions are so very different- nevertheless the fact remains that the functions of a central bank have been found to be best discharged, apparently, in the countries to which I have referred by recourse to the method indicated for the purpose of creating and owning the bank.
I shall not dwell longer upon that point. I am not unmindful of what Sir Thomas White said, but it is only fair to say that Sir Thomas White was opposed to the central bank, and he relied upon the Finance Act as being ample security for the protection of the credit of this country. This is neither the time nor the place to discuss at length a matter which has already been carefully considered in committee. Suffice it to say that the Finance Act, in itself, was an extraordinary expedient to meet an extraordinary circumstance. And with the country off the gold standard, as this country has been since a former Minister of Finance shipped $40,000,000 in gold to the United States-since that time the utilization of the Finance Act offered opportunities for chartered banks such as were not to be found in any other part of

the world, and which need not be here discussed more than to say that any reliance placed upon the observations of the former Minister of Finance to support the proposal in the amendment I believe must be considered in the light of his attitude of mind towards the whole proposal, and cannot be taken as an indication of opinion and separate from the view which he held with respect to the whole matter, as indicated by the report which he made following the proceedings of the Macmillan commission.
My second ground, as I explained to the committee, is I believe of the utmost importance. We had ample evidence during the progress of the discussion in the committee that considerations which govern in the appointment and discharging of the duties and obligations of the bank must have, from the very necessity of things, political consequence. And to make a political football out of a central bank is something which I do not think parliament should ask any body or any government to do. No one who has studied the conditions in this country, and understands them as thoroughly as many hon. gentlemen opposite understand them, will deny that instead of giving the people the broad base for their choice of directors, which they would have if the shareholders as provided by this act were to elect the directors, a proposal looking to a government-selected body of directors, some of whom would hold office during a term necessarily longer than the life of the government, involves considerations in the appointments of a character not conducive to the well-being of the bank. Shall men be appointed to the bank because they reside in a particular locality? Shall men be appointed to the bank because of their occupations? Shall men be appointed to the bank because of their religion? Shall men be appointed to the bank because of their politics? Shall men be appointed to the bank because of their race? Every one of those questions I have put to this committee this afternoon will be asked by every government having the responsibility for the appointment of directors. All you have to do is to look at the commissions and committees set up in this country during the last twenty-five years to realize the soundness of what I have said. Shall a man be appointed as a director of this bank simply to find for him a place because he no longer has a position in his own province? There have been cases in which, in order to find resting places for men no longer useful in their own provinces appointments have been made to important commissions. That is a well known fact. Shall political con-
siderations of that kind prevail, or not? That is the issue. Which is better? Is it better under democratic institutions where you have shares of small value being issued-in this instance shares of $50 each, and where in the selection of shareholders it is intended that there shall be the widest distribution of shares to those who will subscribe for small numbers of shares-which is better, that with the ballot sent to them after nominations have been made they should select the directors for this institution, or shall the considerations to which I have referred be given due weight? Those are considerations which as every hon. member knows provoke effective questions when appointments are to be made by a government. I speak feelingly, and with some small experience. There are hon. members in this house with larger experience. But there is no hon. member who does not know about the pressure which is always exercised with respect to the necessity for finding a place for some man who-and I am not speaking offensively is worn out, tired out or, shall we say, some politician or person who no longer has the opportunity to exercise his powers. These are the facts. I do not wish to mention names, but if I were driven to it I could. All you have to do is to look at the commissions which during the past twenty-five years have been appointed in this country. I am not speaking about one party; I have been very careful not to do that. You will find that the considerations to which I have referred are the considerations which have governed in making appointments.
Not always.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say always; I just simply said that those are the considerations which have governed. There is not an hon. member of this committee within sound of my voice who does not know that that is so.
Might I ask the Prime Minister whether that consideration governed in connection with the appointment of the trustees of the Canadian National Railways?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I explained to the committee the difficulties which were incident to that. The hon. gentleman knows very well what they were. I shall be perfectly frank. The criticism against one gentleman who is serving without salary was that it was not a good thing to have two men of one religion on a committee. That is what was said.

Evidently the Prime
Minister did not permit that criticism to influence his judgment, and quite properly so.

Bank oj Canada

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It did not, but he has been violently criticized because he did not. There are other criticisms which I could mention which were made with respect to other commissions. I am being perfectly frank about this matter of commissions and appointments. I have no hesitation in saying that I should have liked to have approached this question under the conditions that obtain in other countries where there are not the vast areas which we have he_re in Canada and which have not our scattered population. But I realized that I was confronted with facts and not theories and the only method by which this matter could be dealt with as an actual condition in this body politic is the manner in which I have indicated it can be controlled satisfactorily.
I go a step further. How do we propose to elect the directors? Is this to be done by a few gentlemen sitting around a table in the east block? Are they to select them and appoint them? There is to be circulation of ballot papers to every shareholder. These ballot papers will contain the names of the persons nominated and the shareholders, accepting their responsibility, will select seven directors with as much wisdom as they are capable of exercising. That wisdom is good enough to select the hon. members of this parliament who reflect the genius of the Canadian people and it should be sufficiently great to select these directors.
I should like to give an experience I have had in this matter. In the early days of the Northwest Territories we established a law society which was perpetuated by legislation in Alberta and Saskatchewan. When it came to the election of the benchers we provided in the first bill that the benchers should be elected without nomination. Ballot papers were circulated to every member of the profession and he was asked to vote for nine benchers, with the proviso that not more than two should reside in any one judicial district. Strange as it may seem the result was that those who were most prominent at the bar were selected. Later on we provided in Alberta and Saskatchewan that there should be nominations by any three members of the profession. The names of the nominees were printed on a ballot paper, which was sent to each lawyer in the province. Ain addressed envelope was enclosed, upon the back of which was the statement that the ballot was to be returned to the secretary. Again, strangely enough, the leaders of the senior and junior bars were almost in every instance selected by election to fill the positions of benchers, the administrative officers of the law society. We propose
to do just that thing. We propose to put the selection of these directors upon the broadest democratic basis possible. It is not to be put upon the basis of a few gentlemen sitting around a table in the east block to determine who these gentlemen shall be.
Who are the gentlemen to whom the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is referring?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government of the day.
They are responsible to parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, but under the parliamentary institution as we understand it, we know perfectly well that the government must have a majority or it does not exist. That majority sustains the action of the government. I am adopting the broadest democratic basis in permitting the shareholders themselves to select the directors.
The shareholders do not appoint members of the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the broadest basis of democracy. They select by their ballots those who shall be the directors of the bank. That is the method that will be pursued. Nominations will be made and ballots will be distributed and the shareholders of the bank, with a sense of their individual responsibility, will be called upon to vote for seven directors. Each shareholder will be instructed that the directors must not be confined to any one part of the country, that they should represent as many sections of the country and occupations as is possible.
I am not going to follow the argument any further because it has been done at such great length already. I say that it is not correct to describe this bank as a privately owned bank. It is true that there will be shareholders who will pay $50 each for their shares; they will have the right to vote for directors in the manner indicated, but where will rest the control of the bank? Shall the executive officer who must determine its policies be subject to the direction of government? Shall he be forced, as he would be forced in the case of a publicly owned institution, to do what he is told to do by the government of the day? In a moment of political crisis when it is desirable to do a particular thing for party reasons, shall he be subject to that control or shall he be free from such control? He is appointed by the governor in council for a term of years and he knows that his tenure of office depends, not upon the government but upon the extent to which he discharges his
Bank ioj Canada

duties in a manner satisfactory to the people of this country and to the shareholders of the bank. The governor and the deputy governor are to be the executive officers.
Then there is the question of administration. Banks like other institutions are governed by by-laws. By-laws are the rules and regulations under which a concern functions and these will have to be approved iby the governor in council. That is an indication that the government does not undertake to deal with details or with political patronage; it deals with the question only to the extent of approving the governor, the deputy governor and the by-laws that govern. Beyond that the government simply sees that the institution functions and it gives it such assistance as it can give to that end. In order that there shall be close communication and continuity of policy, having regard to the changes of administration in a country such as this, it is provided that the deputy minister shall be a member of the board. He is to have no vote but he is to be there for the purpose of seeing that the government is thoroughly informed as to the conduct and policies of the institution. That is the position there.
I am not going to dwell upon this any longer. In this country there have been many striking illustrations of a commission desiring to do what the government wanted done. There have been many such illustrations during the past fifty years and I think it is desirable that an institution such as this should be freed from such possible criticism.
Lastly, all the profits that are made by this bank, with the exception of $225,000 per year, shall accrue to this country. If the money were found by the Minister of Finance through the consolidated revenue fund it is not improbable that it would cost four per cent, and perhaps more depending upon where it was secured. However, we will say four per cent. Four per cent means $200,000 and the difference between $200,000 and $225,000 is $25,000. I think it will be admitted that that is a very small price to pay for the security which is obtained for the people of this country.
As I said, I shall not traverse the arguments which have been made by the Minister of Finance and myself before the standing committee. In approaching this problem, and it is a very important one in which great responsibility had to be taken by the government of the day, at first blush any hon. member would say:	Yes, a publicly-owned
bank, a bank owned by the country. But when I gave my best attention to the matter, without going again in detail into the reasons 
that influenced my judgment, I could not ask this house to vote for that purpose, and I am not doing so because I believe that if I did I should not be doing what I conceive to be right with respect to the institution which we are now creating and which will play so large a part in shaping the monetary policy of this country.

Before the members of
the committee reach a decision as to which way they will vote on this motion-of course, they have already done so-I would suggest to every one a careful reading of the preamble of this bill. The preamble states quite definitely what will be the functions of the institution which we are creating to-day: Those functions will be to:
-regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare of the dominion.
In other words, we are entrusting the national life of Canada to the body of men who will guide, dominate and control these various functions which are enumerated in the preamble of this bill. Under these circumstances I cannot but agree with the views of Sir Thomas White, who was at one time a distinguished Minister of Finance in this country, who was one of the commissioners appointed by the government to study this question of banking and monetary matters in Canada, who himself stated that he was opposed to the establishment of a central bank and reported against the establishment of such a bank, but who stated emphatically that if there was to be a central bank it should surely be publicly-owned, a bank owned by the people of Canada.
My right hon. friend's argument, if he will allow me to say so, will militate against representative government, at least representative government elected by universal franchise. He asks, "How can a few gentlemen in the east block, instead of the shareholders, control this bank?" Well, the few gentlemen in the east block are the representatives of the people of Canada; they are supposed to be. They are elected by the people of Canada to voice their views and to represent those views in legislation, in administration and otherwise; and when the people of Canada are not satisfied with the representatives whom they have elected, the constitution provides a way to change them.

Bank of Canada

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But their successors cannot change the board.

I beg your pardon. They have the confidence of the people of the country, and I have more confidence in my right hon. friend than he has himself. As against these gentlemen in the east block representing the people of Canada my right hon. friend says that we should prefer the shareholders who select the administrators of that bank. Now, the shareholders cannot be more than 2,000, with the capital which is going to be subscribed and the number of shares which everyone is allowed to own; so that 2,000 people in Canada instead of the government are going to control the economic and national life of the country. Against that principle I will certainly vote. I believe that under the circumstances the central bank, being given the powers which this parliament is giving it, must be publicly-owned. We are taking away from all the private banks which are being operated in Canada the gold which they have in their possession. This institution is going to possess all the gold in Canada, and it will be a privately-owned institution.
I think that if you consider these various elements in connection with this matter you will agree that the motion of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre ought to be accepted by the committee. I am free to admit that I would rather have held the opinion that this should be a privately-owned institution publicly controlled, before I read the bill as it is and heard the discussion and knew all the functions that are going to be those of this public institution. Under the circumstances, the central bank being what it is going to be, I think I should be derelict in my duty if I did not support the principle of public ownership.

When the Prime Minister
announced early in the session that we were to have a central bank I had hoped for two things; one was that the central bank would be given the power to issue all the currency. That is being partially carried out, and my regret is that it is not being carried out 100 per cent. The second was that the bank would be publicly-owned, a bank owned by the people of Canada. Now, I hope I do not prejudice my argument by a fact which is perhaps fairly well known, that in many instances, so far as public services are concerned, I favour public ownership; and I will freely admit that public ownership presents a good many drawbacks. I am not arguing that public ownership is perfect, but I do believe that in many instances
public ownership has nothing to regret when it is compared with the results that have flowed from private ownership. I think the committee and parliament should consider the advantages and disadvantages which may flow from the two separate propositions, private ownership as proposed in the bill, or public ownership as proposed in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.
My reason for saying that this should be a publicly-owned bank is this. I think that entirely too much power is being given to an institution which is not publicly-owned. I do not suppose I need to review these powers. Some of them have already been referred to; perhaps not all. In the first place the bank will be given the power of issuing currency, a great power. Again, it will have possession of all the gold in the country, amounting to $107,000,000. Again it will have in its possession five per cent of all the deposits in the chartered banks; it will have the reserves which have been put aside for certain purposes in the banks; it will have the repayment of advances made under the Finance Act and it will-and this is perhaps more important than any of the other features-[DOT] have control of the credit of Canada. I was going to say-and this is more or less by the way-that this bank, especially if it were privately owned might be given some additional powers; it might have control of the reserves, for instance, of insurance companies and of trust funds in various organizations, pension funds, and perhaps later on, when we establish, if we do an unemployment insurance scheme those funds might also very well be administered by this bank.
I may be wrong but I am credibly informed that this central bank will actually have in its control and possession funds amounting to the stupendous sum of between $300,000,000 and $500,000,000. That .is a tremendous power to give to a privately owned institution. I cannot quite agree with the Prime Minister when he says that it is not correct to describe this bank as a privately owned one. After all it is a privately owned bank and although the number of shareholders will be comparatively small, some 2,000 and no one of them-
The hon. member's mathematics is bad. It is 20,000.

I was repeating for the
moment what the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) had said. Let us, however, say 20,000 persons. I am not going to dwell on this to any great extent but I believe it is possible to concentrate, by way of
Bank tof Canada

having the shares held in trust, a great deal of power in a few hands in the ownership of the shares of this bank.
Something was said also-and this was said in the committee-that ownership of the bank by private persons might lead to a great deal of external influence being exercised upon it. I need only read what Sir Thomas White, one of the commissioners, said. This is what he said:
It is also my view that a central bank of Canada should not be empowered except with the approval of parliament, to enter into agreements with other central banks which would undoubtedly, on account of their greater experience and wide sources of information, possess decided advantage in the negotiation of such agreements.
More than that-and I think this is important-Mr. Beaudry Leman, also one of the commissioners-and I do not think he can be accused of being a great advocate of public ownership-had this to say:
Measures calculated to develop intra-imperial cooperation, as set forth in paragraph number 211, should not be developed beyond the scope of providing ample facilities for the interchange of goods and services, unless the people of Canada understand and decide, in full knowledge of the consequences, that close monetary cooperation may lead to close economic association which in turn is a step towards common political action.
I am not attributing any sinister motives whatever to the Prime Minister or to the government in deciding finally that the bank shall be privately owned. The Prime Minister Stated-and I believe he is quite sincere-that at first blush, as he put it, he was in favour of having this a publicly owned bank. I wish he had adhered to that view, because I believe it to be true that there would be greater public confidence in a publicly owned than in a privately owned bank, restricted though it may be in its powers. The other day the Minister of Finance, in explaining this bill and the Prime Minister again to-day, made reference to central banks in other countries and in most instances those are privately owned. Banks like the Bank of England and the Bank of France are the growth of perhaps a number of centuries and those are older countries. I am afraid, unlike some of my friends the lawyers, I am not necessarily a great believer in precedents. Someone once said: We make our own precedents, and I believe we can make progress in all things and need not necessarily look to older countries for the course we ought to adopt. For example, in the United States, one of the newer countries if you like, this year there was introduced into congress a bill which provided for a number of things. This bill was sponsored by the two senior members

of the committee, Congressmen Stegall and Goldsborough, two prominent members of the United States congress. This is the kind of bank they proposed:
It would set up a federal monetary authority which would have sole custody of the nation's metallic currency reserves, power to regulate credit and, at the end of three years, the exclusive right to issue currency in the United States. As stated in details these powers correspond identically with the essential functions of any central bank.
This proposed institution was to supersede the federal reserve bank system as they now have- it in the United States. The article goes on:
The "authority" itself would consist of seven directors to be appointed by the president with Senate approval. They would- be representative of agriculture, industry and banking, and would be headed by a governor and deputy governors after the manner of a central bank. They would be subject to removal from office only by the president or by congress, but would be debarred from any private interest in finance, manufacturing or foreign trade.
The authority would thus be free from any control except that of the government; and any profits from its operations would, after deductions for reserves, go to the treasury.
I cite that merely as an argument against accepting the theory, if you like, that we must necessarily follow the practice of the older banks in the older countries.
There has been only one real objection advanced to having this bank publicly owned and that ds the danger or supposed danger referred to by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that in the appointment of directors and in the conduct of the bank itself especially-and I think the Minister of Finance said this-if an election were in prospect, political influence would be brought to bear upon the conduct of the bank. I have said before in the house and also in the committee on banking and commerce that I am surprised and disappointed that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister himself should have so little confidence in the public men and the democracy of this country. Public men are constantly being criticized more I think in jest than in earnest that they are out to serve their own ends as members of parliament. I do not think that is borne out by the fact but certainly if we, the government of this country, say that we are not to be trusted, what can we expect from those who elected us? The Prime Minister has referred to the difficulties in making appointments, to the fact that certain interests have to be considered, such as language, religion, geography and ail the rest. He spoke a moment ago about the criticism which he received because he appointed two members of a certain faith

Bank of Canada
to the national railway board. My answer to that is this: Surely a government has backbone enough, as it had in that case, to resist any unjust demands that are made upon it. Therefore in the final analysis these would be my reasons for wanting the bank publicly owned. In the first place, it is entirely too great a power to be placed in the hands of private individuals; in the second, a central bank will have the confidence of the people of Canada to a much greater degree if it is publicly rather than privately owned, especially in view of the facts which have been disclosed before various committees of the house. For these reasons I am going to support the amendment.

I wish to express in a feiw words my sentiments on this, to my mind, very important departure in Canadian history. May I say first that I am a private ownership man. As far as possible I believe in private ownership. But having regard to the preamble, which after all is the guiding principle of the whole bill, I cannot help but tell this house the reason I am supporting one hundred per cent the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). I was surprised to hear the arguments of the Prime Minister concerning the method of electing directors, and I wish to say a few words on that. Is there any man in this house who thinks that a cabinet representing all the people of Canada-not only those who are able to subscribe $2,500-[DOT] and having the confidence, as they should have, of the people of Canada as a whole, are not in a better position to select the men who are to control the financial policy and the national credit of Canada than 2,000 shareholders whose only qualification is that they were able to put up $2,500? I am sure that there is not any serious-minded person who will say that the men in the first category are not much better able to select proper directors to manage that institution than the shareholders as provided under the act.
Then I wish to say a word in connection with the gold situation. This institution is to have the control of all the gold of Canada. Furthermore it is to confiscate the gold of the private banks of Canada. I know that legal justification may be asserted for this, but I do not believe it is the proper thing to confiscate the property of any citizen and to hand that property over to another citizen. If we are going to have confiscation let us have it for the benefit of the state and no one else.
Then this institution is to have, progressively I will admit, but eventually, the entire control of the issue of money in Can-74726-263
ada. In view of the Prime Minister's changed attitude as to the money policy of this government as expressed in this house yesterday I begin to think it is most important that we should have a governmentally owned institution, or at least an institution controlled by the government, to manage safely the national credit in the interests of all the people of Canada. Then I submit another suggestion. Under the present legislation we have a treasury board acting under the Finance Act. With conditions as they are to-day I do not think any member of parliament should vote in favour of a system which in any way will lessen the present powers of the treasury board under the Finance Act. I believe that by this new institution we are lessening the powers of the treasury board. Then there is another argument as to the selection of the officers of the institution. I support the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) in his statement. When I want land surveyed, although I cannot rim a line I can hire a man to dio the job for me and can tell him where I want it run. I do not think this parliament has any reason to take second place to the business men of this country. The managements of our privately owned banks in Canada have been able to select men to manage their institutions, not perhaps in the interest of all the people of Canada, but at least in the interest of their shareholders. In spite of the fact that some of the directors, in fact many of them, are not at all qualified to manage those institutions, they are able to hire such men as Mr. Wilson, Mr. Logan and many others who have been successful in conducting banks for the benefit of their shareholders. Surely eighteen selected men-selected men, I say- out of a population of over ten million, are competent to hire officers who can manage this institution, especially when it is to be charged with responsibility-and I want to read it into Hansard because I think it is most important-
-to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare of the dominion.
Furthermore, at present we have a privately owned system of note issue, which is covered at all times by assets to a varying degree. Under this new legislation we are handing over to the Bank of Canada, the absolute power of note issue for the whole Dominion of Canada. In view of these considerations, and after listening to the argument of the Prime Minister, I cannot see how any hon.

Bank oj Canada

member on either side of the house-I am uot speaking politically-can take any other stand than that the control of the national credit of Canada should be in the hands of people representing Canada or in the hands of the government of the country.

I had not intended to take any part in this discussion, but in view of what has been said I think a few remarks would not be out of place, giving my own views and the views of those with whom I am associated. First I should like to say that every view that has been presented here this afternoon was presented with force and power by gentlemen who I have no doubt honestly held the views they expressed. I give them credit for honest and honourable intentions, and they are quite justified in expressing their views. I must confess that I am rather surprised to find the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) in the role of a supporter of public ownership. I have never heard that heretofore he has been included in that category. But there is always time for repentance. Personally, I am not a proponent of public ownership; I am not doing any violence to my conscience when I vote for private ownership in the sense in which it is restricted and limited by this bill. But certain statements have been made here to-day which I do not think are quite borne out by the facts. In the first place the hon. member for Quebec East said that the board of directors of this bank would be elected by 2,000 shareholders. That would be true if only 2.000 people should become shareholders of the bank, which would be possible having regard to the limitations imposed by the bill. But it is equally possible that there will be 100.000 shareholders, having regard to the announced policy of the government that the shares shall be distributed as widely as possible. So I suggest to my hon. friend that while his mathematics may be technically correct they are not practically correct.
Public ownership of any great and important utility is a great idea. But I have never seen a country yet where it worked out one hundred per cent, not even in the great province of Ontario.

You cannot expect one hundred per cent.
* Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): Certainly it has not worked out in connection with the railways of this country. For the reasons which have been alleged already I am going to support the principle of private ownership of this bank, as I think the committee would be well advised to do.

It has been stated here to-day that pressure would be brought to bear upon the government of the day in regard to creeds and sections throughout the country. I can show you a file of correspondence in my office coming from various parts of the country demanding that a certain number of the directors of this bank shall be chosen from one race in this country. There are many resolutions couched in exactly the same language,, showing the propaganda that is going on. That is one evidence. I will not mention the race; hon. gentlemen can draw their own conclusions. This indicates that the moment anything of this sort is set up there is a reaction of this kind in the minds of some people. Does that tend to strengthen the position of' the institution? I humbly submit that it does not. Then there is the question of sectionalism. Did we ever set up a board of directors for the national railways when sectionalism was not a paramount consideration?" I put that to hon. gentlemen opposite. They know it and we know it, and that does not make for the best cooperation possible. I think it is one of the great weaknesses of Canada that we are governed by sectionalism. We are bound to consider the different sections of the country; otherwise we would not have a maritime position on one question, a central Canada position on another and a western position on another. This is an embarrassment and a detriment to the proper-government of the country. We must admit that the principle of governing the country according to sectionalism is wrong, and surely the same principle should apply to the bank.

My hon. friend referred to the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. Is he contending now that the present board was appointed with the idea of giving expression to the wishes of these various factions?

No, I do not say that, but I say that the board set up in 1922 or 1923, which went out of office in 1930, and the board set up in lieu thereof in 1930 or 1931 gave expression to this sectionalism in Canada, and it was very hard to operate the board because of the diverse interests that were represented.
But that does not applj*- to the present board?

No, it does not, because, as I understand it, that principle was discarded in the appointment of the trustees, of whom there are only three under the statute.

Bank of Canada
Surely the experience of other countries is of value; surely it is not a crime to follow the example of England, although in the minds of some members of this house it may be so considered. They have had a privately owned central bank, the Bank of England, ever since they have had a central bank. It has performed exactly the functions that are intended to be performed by this bank. More than that, in the great majority of cases where central banks have been set up in other countries, invariably and with very minor and few exceptions those banks have been privately owned in the same sense that this bank is to be privately owned. Why is that? Hon. gentlemen in this house should pause and query why that has been the case. In Canada we have reason to know why there might be interference with a bank if it were publicly owned. I can visualize what might happen, and it is to guard against that sort of thing that this institution has been set up in this way.
I should like to pay some attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) with respect to the gold question. Very incorrectly, in my judgment, he said there would be confiscation of *the gold of the private banks. If I understand the word in its proper meaning, confiscation is taking without compensation. There is no such intention or underlying principle in this bill. The gold of the chartered banks is to be taken over, save and except that portion of it required for the external obligations of the banks, and due compensation is to be made. I did not understand that the banks as such objected *to the taking over of their gold, because they admitted that gold was no longer necessary as part of their reserves. the public ownership of financial institutions I am very glad to welcome these gentlemen to the ranks of public ownership.

There are some fine advances made in the measure now before us, and even if I cannot have all the amendments I should like, I certainly will vote for the bill when it comes up for third reading.
For a moment or two let me remark upon the arguments advanced by the Prime Minister. He set forth three arguments, the first being that the experience of the world would lead us to adopt the present form of private ownership of banks. In that connection may I observe that the experience of the world has been very meagre, in the matter of public ownership of banks, and secondly that all the experience of private ownership of banks has not been attractive. The methods adopted in financing, in other countries of the world, and especially during the period of and since the great war, as I say has not been attractive. Indeed, the mismanagement of the financial institutions by private corporations in various countries of the world has led to the necessity for the legislation now before the committee. I do not think we can draw our inspiration even from the historic old Bank of England in handling the financial affairs of the British nation, especially during the past decade or so.
Then, the second point made by the Prime Minister was that of having freedom from political control. I do not believe there is anything under heaven free from political control. I do not believe we can have anything free from political control. While I agree with what the Prime Minister said- and I state that so far as it went his argument in that connection was very forceful,

indeed-I think his argument was more of an indictment of the present parliamentary system than an argument against the public ownership of banks. I would say that there is only too much truth in what he said. So far as the party system is concerned-and perhaps we will not get the full working of the social ownership of banks until the C.C.F. comes into power-nevertheless, as I have said on many occasions, I would rather have bank governors and directors appointed by the Prime Minister or by the leader of the opposition than by any group of private bankers we might find anywhere.
The third point was that the presently proposed bank is really, in fact, a public institution, inasmuch as the government has the appointment of the governor and certain [DOT]functionaries of the institution. Of course, there is truth in this, that the private control of the banks is in many respects very strictly limited, and that those features of the bill are of course acceptable as a bill providing for a private institution. But the fact remains that the entire control of the central financial institution of this country is being reposed in a private concern. In my opinion that is not a wise thing to do and I would urge that the Prime Minister who, as he says himself, believes or had the opinion at the outset that the proper thing to do was to make this a government bank in reality, would give further consideration to the arguments which have been put forward this afternoon, and that he will make this bank wholly and entirely a socially owned, nationally owned, publicly owned-whichever term you desire to use-institution, so that we may control, and so that the financial policies of the country may be in the hands of the representatives of the Canadian people. I would point out to the Prime Minister that if under government control poor governors were appointed, governors who were incapable of carrying out their duties, we certainly would have direct recourse and ultimately, at least, could effect the necessary improvements by removing the incapable officials and appointing others in their places. But under a private institution we will have no such power. They will find their own governors and their own directors who will do business in the way they want them to do it. I urge that further consideration be given, and that the amendment be accepted.

Don't be so anxious. Hon. gentlemen opposite are quite free to express their opinions, and I claim the right to express mine. I am opposed to the amendment for the very reason advanced for its adoption by the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), namely the provisions in the preamble of the bill under which the Bank of Canada can control the credit and currency, meaning the commercial credit and currency, necessary for carrying on the ordinary business of the country. As between a privately owned and controlled institution, with all the safeguards thrown around it by this bill, and a politically controlled institution which would govern the credit provided the business interests of this country, I must favour the privately controlled, or privately owned, publicly controlled and, if you like, privately managed institution for which there is provision in this bill. As a matter of fact, I would go farther than the bill has gone, and in addition to setting up a stock issue of $5,000,000 in shares of $50 each, or whatever they may be when the bill has passed, I would in addition make an issue of common shares representing a small proportion of the total capital of the bank, with the provision that the persons who purchased those shares, whether or not they be the same persons who purchased the preferred shares, would have an added interest in the success of the institution by the further possibility of sharing with the state the profits accruing to the State. Under the provisions of this bill the profits, such as they are, or whatever they may be, accrue one hundred per cent to the state, and when hon. members talk about the institution being managed, and talk about confiscation being effected to the advantage of private individuals they overlook entirely the fact that as now provided all of the profits arising out of the operation of this bank accrue to the state. When we
look at the experience which this country has had and is now having with publicly owned and directly parliamentary controlled institutions, we cannot hope to have an independent institution so long as it remains within the hands of any government, no matter what side of politics it may be on. A politically controlled bank could destroy the industry of this country in six months through unwise actions. That possibility rests within the provisions of the bill.
What has been our experience with our national railways? The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has left the chamber but he knows what that experience has been. The first board of directors of the Canadian National Railways were still holding office when the government was changed in 1922. When the new government came into office the president and the entire board were dismissed and a new political board appointed. As was testified to by the then president, Sir Henry Thornton, that board continued to operate in a political manner. The commission which investigated the whole situation used the term, "the thin red line of political activity." We have a similar situation to-day in the province of Ontario. The management of one of the greatest publicly owned institutions are to be dismissed and political appointees put in their places. What guarantee have we that the same thing would not happen in the case of this bank? Should there be a change of government, the governor, the deputy governor and the board of directors who controlled, this great central bank would be automatically dismissed.

Will not the hon. gentleman admit that the hydro commission of Ontario, a publicly owned institution, has saved the people of that province hundreds of millions of dollars when it is considered what they would have had to pay for power had it been owned by private parties?

At the moment I am not discussing the merits of hydro electric in Ontario; I am discussing the management. The governor, the deputy governor and the directors of a bank such as the central bank of Canada is to be should not be subject to political dismissal. I grant that a government may be trusted to find the best men available for these positions, but there can be no continuity of policy or that direction which is required in the managing of an institution of this kind when the governor and all the officers are subject to dismissal when a political change occurs. My hon. friend knows that the whole organization of the hydro electric in Ontario is to be subject to political dismissals.

I desire to move an
amendment to clause 6, subclause 2, by substituting in paragraph (a) the words "Canadian national" in place of "British subject." This amendment is seconded by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dubuc).
In order to avoid any misunderstanding as to the meaning of "Canadian national," I wish to refer first to an act of parliament passed in 1921 defining a Canadian national. In that year Mr. Doherty, then Minister of Justice, thought it advisable to define by statute what constituted a Canadian national, and it was defined as follows:
The following persons are Canadian nationals, viz:-(a) any British subject who is a Canadian citizen within the meaning of the Immigration Act.
That is to say, who has Canadian domicile; and a Canadian domicile is acquired by having in Canada for at least five years a residence as his permanent abode,
I want to call the attention of members of the committee to the difference between clause 10, which deals with the qualification of the directors of the bank, and clause 6, which deals with the qualifications of the governor, the deputy governor and the assistant deputy governor. To be a director of the bank, one
must be necessarily a British subject ordinarily resident in Canada, while in the case of the governor, the deputy governor and the assistant deputy governor, one need only be a British subject. In view of this difference it is obvious that the government had it in mind to select the three last mentioned officers from outside Canada and when the Prime Minister was attending the committee on banking and commerce he made no secret of it. To this I am opposed, and the purpose of my amendment is to ensure the appointment of a Canadian. Why should it be otherwise?
Canada first.

Clause 6 states that the governor and deputy governor shall be men of proven banking experience; under the bill, this is the only qualification required, so far as competency is concerned. Have we not in Canada men of proven banking experience? What are the facts? Not so long ago, while in the United States we had the alarming situation of every bank temporarily suspending payment, ours stood firm. While during the last ten years, more than 9,000 banks in the United States failed, is it not a significant fact that in Canada, during the last twenty years only one bank went into liquidation? Do not these facts sufficiently prove the ability and efficiency which have characterized the administration of our banks?
What took place in England from 1928 to 1931? The bankers of England and of the United States borrowed money from the bankers of France and made loans to Germany. Subsequently Germany repudiated her debts and the consequence is that large sums of money were lost by those bankers of England and the United States. No such thing has happened in Canada, and the least I can say is that we have no lesson to learn from those bankers.
More than that, Lord Macmillan, the head of the royal commission which conducted the investigation into our banking system, is reported as having expressed the view that Canadian bankers were men of integrity, high character and high efficiency. Why should we now question the capability of their management? The Prime Minister while before the committee on banking and commerce said: W7e have no Canadian with the necessary knowledge to operate a central bank.

To act in the best interests of a nation one must know those interests thoroughly. To promote, as ex-piessed in the preamble, the economic and financial welfare of the dominion, one must know the economic conditions of this country. As the Prime Minister said, conditions vary from one country to another. They are not the same here as they are in England. And there are many other factors which have to be taken into consideration.
If this bank is to operate for the benefit of Canada and no other country, it is essential that those who manage it should know best what is good for Canada, that they should be persons who know the domestic and industrial requirements of the country. Canadian financial men are more competent to deal with such matters than any distinguished gentlemen from outside who do not know our local conditions. Bank of Canada

Is it going to be a branch of the Bank of England, dominated by the Bank of England?
