The determination of our credit and financial policy should be vested in the hands of Canadians, who are best acquainted with the needs of Canada. We have in Canada distinguished Canadian bankers, thoroughly versed in the economic and banking conditions of the country, who have intimate knowledge of our needs, and it will be not only to the detriment of Canada but an insult to Canadian citizens if we appoint officers from outside Canada to manage this bank.

In supporting this motion
I shall add but one word, directing the attention of the committee to the important fact that the economic control of the country means unquestionably the political control. Canadians certainly can buy the experience that it has been said in the committee that possibly none of us possess. The board of directors of all our banks, which have had the success mentioned here to-day, have found general managers and men to administer those banks who had experience which the directors did not have. Surely this central bank, which is to be the foundation of the entire fabric of our economic life, should be controlled nationally and not privately. The management is to be in the hands of the committee of three; the board of directors will only give them advice. If those three gentlemen, or two of them, are from another country, surely the danger is great. Canadians should always preserve autonomy in and keep control of our economic affairs, because to fail to do so would also mean the abandonment and loss of our political autonomy. Mr. Chairman, this is a very important fact to which I invite the attention of this parliament and of the public of Canada.

I have listened with some interest to the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite. At the moment we are not appointing gentlemen to fill any offices. There is a limitation placed by the bill upon the nationality of the person or persons who may be appointed to such offices. I think the only desire that animated those who prepared the bill was to provide this country with the best possible officers in the first years of the bank's operation. Not many years ago, when the city of Paris installed electric tramways, it
sent to Montreal for a man skilled in the operation of electric railways, one Duncan McDonald, who went to Paris 'and there carried out in a thoroughly satisfactory way the organization of that system. We have frequently had to go beyond our own frontiers to find skilled and experienced men to guide our enterprises in their infancy. Hon. gentlemen will recall that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was founded those who were interested in its management sent to the United States and brought here Mr. Van Horne and Mr. Shaughnessy, afterwards Lord Shaugh-nessy. They will also recall that just a few years ago, when the best man available was being sought to coordinate the Canadian National railways, hon. gentlemen opposite, despite the fact that in Canada we had great experience in railway matters, deemed it wise to go to Great Britain to find Sir Henry Thornton.
Do you consider that was a success?

That may have depended upon the quality of judgment which was exercised by those who were in office, but it by mo means undermines the principle by which that selection was made. That principle is all that is at stake here. We are seeking to get people who have experience in the administration of an organization of this kind, and for that reason it has not been restricted to Canada where such an organization never has been operated, and where it may be said no one, however skilled he may be in commercial banking, has ever had the duty of operating a central bank. These, I think, are some reasons which might well be considered by the committee when determining what form this section should take.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I intend to say only a few words. I do deprecate the introduction into this discussion on every occasion of matters such as that raised by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymond). When it is not the Bank of England it is something else, always something savouring of nationalism.
Canada first.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly, and I shall presently point out exactly what that means. It is so evident that this is done in a desire to obscure discussion by appeals to prejudice, which I think is to be very much deprecated. The red thread runs through this whole discussion, and I see it with dismay and regret.
I have listened to this discussion with regard tc Canadians. I think probably I have
Bank oj Canada

as high regard for Canadian ability as any man in this committee, ajnd I have acted upon that opinion. But occasionally governments desire to have a dispassionate view of a situation. That was in the mind of the right hon. leader of the opposition when Sir Andrew Rae Duncan was brought here for the purpose of making a report on matters of transcendent importance to three provinces. He was chairman; his recommendations involved this country in very large annual expenditures. The successful effort to bring him here was not criticized, I am bound to say, and when the right hon. gentleman chose Sir Henry Thornton as head of the railways that choice met with the approval of at least one member of this chamber in addition to himself; that was myself. Sir Henry Thornton was a naturalized British subject, but not a resident of Canada. But I have higher authority than that, which I am sure will appeal to the hon. member for Beauharnois. I hold in my hand a speech made on the lottery issue by Premier Taschereau of Quebec, and in the next to last paragraph I find these words:
I do not know how we would organize if allowed to have a lottery. We could perhaps have a man attached to the French national lottery come here and advise us as to the organization work here.
He would not necessarily leave him in control for many years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If those who are now speaking will permit the hon. member for Beauharnois to ask his question I should be glad to answer it.

I did not know that Premier Taschereau had taken the trouble of going to someone else for advice, as the Prime Minister did in this case, when he asked the advice of Lord Macmillan as to the experience of our Canadian financial men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am just about to finish the quotation; I have not read the part of it in which I am particularly interested:
That was the procedure that we adopted when we created our system of provincial statistics, which is the best in Canada.
To get advice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is exactly the basis of what I am endeavouring to say. The hon. gentleman has said that we have bankers in Canada who are equal to any bankers in the world. Yet there is not one general manager of a bank in Canada who would undertake this position. I put it to them in the committee; I asked them right then and there, and what is more I know it, not from hearsay 
but from definite statements. They are of the opinion that we have no one in this country yet trained in central bank experience, and if Mr. Taschereau found it necessary to send to Paris to get someone to teach him how to gather statistics, with all the men we have in this country trained in audits and statistics, with all the magnificent brains we have and the certificates tjjey have obtained from various parts of the country; if -the premier of Quebec found it necessary to establish his system by bringing in someone from France, would it be a violation of sound judgment if someone assisted these men to establish the central bank?
Is that the reason-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The jumping jacks might sit down; I was not pushing the button at that moment.
Now just one further word. This act contemplates a successful central bank; this act contemplates the central bank being placed, in the first instance, in charge of someone who has some knowledge or experience in that regard. I should like to know what experience any banker in Canada has had with regard to central banks. I have asked every general manager who has had to do with the management of these banks, and not one of them has had any experience nor yet understands and realizes all that is involved in central banks. In commercial banking our bankers are equal to any in the world; in fact the large United States banks draw from the personnel of our chartered banks from time to time because of their high qualities, their experience and their training. But when it comes down to the question of a central bank we have no one that can lead. Whoever undertakes the responsibility as head of this central bank must have some knowledge in the first instance in order to give whatever Canadian is appointed the necessary and requisite experience to carry on his job. Just as Mr. Taschereau had to send to France to get someone to teach him statistics so it is proposed, by this government at least, that someone shall teach Canadians how to carry on with respect to central banks.
It is intended that this bank shall be managed, controlled and operated by Canadians; it has no more relation to the Bank of England than any other central bank in the world has to that bank. It will have to do business with the Bank of England; to hon. gentlemen opposite that is an offence. It will have to do business with the Bank of France, with the Bank of Germany, with the Bank of Austria and with the central banks

Bank oj Canada
of all the countries of the world with which the trade and commerce of Canada is carried on. Without anticipating the appointment I can only say that whoever undertakes this work, whoever is appointed, must get experience. He will have to spend some time after his appointment in studying central bank conditions throughout the world. He will have to learn what is to be done and how it is to be done. There is no contact between the management of the central bank and the individual except as he is affected by the policies of the central bank. If hon. gentlemen opposite had taken the trouble to inquire into the relations between the Bank of France and the provincial and city banks of France and between the Bank of England and the chartered banks of that country, as I have, I think they would realize that the qualities required in the governor of a central bank are just as far removed from the qualities required of the successful general manager of a commercial bank as are the qualities that fit a lawyer, for instance, to give legal advice as compared with one who has had no experience or training in the law at all. Why do we seek technicians? Why do we ask the assistance of technicians-not brain trusts, but technicians? Why do we do that? Because their training fits them to give advice which may be of assistance. I say to this committee, frankly, that this bank could not successfully be established without some training and assistance being given, training derived by the gentleman who is appointed spending his time in securing it, or assistance given for a limited time by someone who has knowledge of it. It could not otherwise successfully be created or set up. About that fact bankers have no doubt.-none of them. And these same bankers to whom the hon. member for Beauharnois referred, tell me that there are not in this country the trained minds to set up a central bank. And there is not one of them, I challenge the hon. gentleman-not a general manager in this country-but who will say that.

Rough on our
bankers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not a bit of it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before this amendment is put to a vote I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymand) not only upon his proposal but upon the argument he put forth in its support. I might say that the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) at the opening of his speech do not lessen in any way the value of the proposal and argument of the hon. member for Beauharnois. It is unfortunate that an hon. member cannot suggest something of this kind without being charged with arousing prejudices. As far as I am concerned, I intend to support this proposal in apite of the charges made.
What is wrong with the proposal? The bill provides that the directors of this bank must be Canadians; the shareholders must be Canadians, and the hon. member for Beauharnois is simply asking that the same principle should apply to the governor and deputy governor. Section 14 of the bill gives supreme authority to the governor. No decision of the board of directors can have any value unless it is approved by the governor; he is the supreme master. Surely when such powers are being given to an institution, powers such as were mentioned this afternon and are enumerated in the preamble, it should not be considered as extraordinary to ask that these officers should be Canadians. Is there anything new in this proposal? My right hon. friend referred to nationalism in connection with this matter, but I should like to refer him to a book entitled Central Banks by Kisch and Elkin. In looking through this publication I find that the charter of the national bank of Yugoslavia provides that the governor and deputy governors must be subjects of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and reside in Belgrade. In Italy, all the members of the board, the general manager and his deputy must be Italian subjects. In Germany, the president and the members of the managing board must be Germans. The same provision will be found in the charters of other central banks, and such a provision is not unreasonable in connection with this bank.
We are vesting in this institution powers which concern the economic life of our country. It is to look after credit, currency, employment and practically everything concerning our economic life. We are even giving to the bank certain powers which are now in the hands of the government. We are taking from the government certain powers which are very important and placing them in the hands of this institution. Under these circumstances, I think that any self-respecting people would see that the men who are to have supreme control over such an institution should be citizens of their own country. Any-
Bank of Canada

one who makes such a proposal to the House of Commons of Canada should not be charged with arousing prejudices. I do not think my right hon. friend was serious when he compared this matter with the fact that Mr. Taschereau of Quebec had stated that before a lottery was set up he would have someone in France acquainted with the operation of lotteries come over and advise him. I have no objection to the governor or the board of directors of this bank calling for expert advice from England or anywhere else, but I do *object to the governor or the deputy governor of this bank not being Canadians. When my right hon. friend stated that this central bank probably would have to do business with the Bank of England, the Bank of France, the Bank of Italy and other banks, he was offering a strong argument for the appointment of a Canadian and not someone from the Bank of England. As the bill now stands, I assume it would have to be a gentleman from the Bank of England because he must be a British subject. I do not see where my right hon. friend could get a governor with sufficient experience except from the Bank of England, but I still contend that the governor and deputy governor should be Canadians. There are Canadians who are qualified for these positions just as they are qualified to be prime minister of Canada.

I am sorry to have to prolong this debate, but in a few words I desire to place myself on record as being in favour of this amendment. May I say in all sincerity that I was amazed to find out this afternoon that at least some part of a speech of Mr. Taschereau had convinced the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). Apparently the speech as a whole did not mean much to him, but he took a few sentences w'hich suited his purpose in connection with this bill. I agree with the opinion of the Minister of Justice-
The former Minister of Justice.

-the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and the future Minister of Justice, that there is no comparison to be made between the organization of a lottery in Canada and this very important institution. It might as well be said that because we import coaches to teach cricket to the sportsmen of this country, or, as has been the habit lately, American coaches for rugby, this would be an argument in favour of the governor of the central bank being a British subject. He would probably be from

England and this bank would be an annex: of the Bank of England.
In a further section it is provided that the governor, the deputy governor and the assistant deputy governor are to be appointed for seven years. It is true there is a reservation that the first governor may be appointed by the government for a shorter period; but if I am to judge by the remarks made this-afternoon by the Prime Minister, and if we are remiss in anything connected with central banking operations in Canada, I am very much afraid that what the Prime Minister has in mind is not only to appoint a man from Great Britain to be governor, but that very likely he will allow his term to run the full period of seven years, as provided in the bill. This concerns not only the governor but also the deputy governor and the assistant deputy governor. So that this is not going to be a central bank of Canada but rather a branch in Canada of the Bank of England.

The Bank of England
in Canada.

If we deal with banks
in other countries we shall therefore be in a very humiliating position when it is found that the representatives of this country on the central bank of Canada had to be imported from somewhere else because we have no one in Canada who could undertake the duties.
The hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymond) has quoted from the commission which led to the establishment of this bank. I am quite convinced that we have in Canada bankers who are fully equipped to undertake the work. They might be advised by experts, as suggested, but it is not so much the technique of central banking that is important as it is the influence that will be vested in these-gentlemen; and I think that influence should remain wholly Canadian. The Prime Minister has said that the bankers themselves have suggested that there is no one able to take the position.
There is no evidence of that.

Well, I know of many
bankers in Montreal who would advise the-Prime Minister to drop the bill altogether. But he will take the advice of such bankers as suits his purpose, in the same way as he has culled a few sentences from Mr. Tas-chereau's speqch because they happen to suit him. He will not pay any attention, how

ever, to anyone except those who advise him to do the very things that he has defied them to do before taking their advice. We are

Bank oj Canada
taking the proper stand to-night and I congratulate my good friend from Beauharnois on his amendment. If there is any institution in Canada that should be Canadian, that institution in my opinion is the proposed Bank of Canada; otherwise Bank of Canada is a misnomer and will lead us nowhere. Personally, owing probably to my environment in Montreal, I have no strong faith in this institution, but that faith will be weakened if I find that it is not a Canadian bank at all but merely a branch of a bank in some other part of the empire.
May I point this out further without any desire to offer personal criticism. I think that if this amendment had not been moved the house would not have been aware that the Prime Minister had already decided not to appoint a Canadian to the position. That is very much the case with this government in many other instances; unless they are pressed by our opposition we are not told what certain measures actually involve. In this instance, if it were only that it brought out a clear statement from the Prime Minister that he would not appoint a Canadian banker to the position of governor, I think the amendment was worth while and I hope that the committee will vote affirmatively on it. Indeed, it deserves exactly the same vote as the one we had this afternoon on the introduction of another bill; we should be unanimous in our desire that the governor of the central bank should be a Canadian.

The four speakers on this side who have previously spoken in favour of the amendment are all from the province of Quebec. I assure the committee that, coming from British Columbia, I am in full accord with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymond). And I speak not only as a western Canadian but as a Scottish-born Canadian when I say I have no desire to tie up the Bank of Canada as an apanage of the Bank of England.
You are no colonial.

There
were two gentlemen of the Bank of England 

Messrs. Kershaw and Fisher-who accompanied the Macmillan commission on its travels throughout Canada. After the mission was completed a dinner was given for Lord Macmillan in Canada House in England and very significant statements were made there in regard to the future governance of the Bank of Canada and the dominance of Bank of England policies in our Canadian bank.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not correct. Just read what was said.

I am
quoting from Hansard, page 1319.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: From what?

From
Hansard, to which reference had been made,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
made a statement in regard to what was said in Canada House. I ask him to read it.

I shall
be glad to produce the press extract on a future occasion for the benefit of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
statement is not correct.

These
two gentlemen, I say, accompanied the com* mission throughout Canada. They were never mentioned in the press nor were their activities heralded, and so far as I am concerned. I want this Bank of Canada to be a Canadian-controlled bank and Canadian-directed, by a Canadian. My right hon. friend made the cry of Canada first ring from shore to shore in this dominion in 1930. So far as this Bank of Canada is concerned, I say Canada only and all for Canada. The right hon. gentleman this afternoon mentioned some statement of Premier Taschereau in regard to lotteries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With regard to statistics.
Statistics-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And lotteries.

I took
down the Prime Minister's statement as he spoke and I shall be borne out by Hansard, that he used the word "lotteries" in connection with the quotation he made in this house. He said that Premier Taschereau had imparted someone from another country to>
advise him.
Would import.

Would import. Now, I agree with the Prime Minister in this, that if there is necessity for technical experts in connection with the Bank of Canada expert advice should be given, and we will support him to the limit in getting from the Bank of England or the Bank of France or any other central bank all the technical advisers, at good salaries, who are' necessary' for the inauguration of the Bank of Canada. But we do say' that a bank that is
Bank oj Canada

going to control $107,000,000 of .the people's gold; a bank that is going to take over $40,000,000 from the private banks of Canada; a bank that is going to have securities amounting to $63,000,000, on which the taxpayers of Canada are going to pay $1,800,000 a year in interest; a bank that is going to take over deposits of chartered banks at five per cent; a bank that will have a total asset value on the day i.t opens its doors of over $300,000,000, is an institution over which no Englishman or Scotchman or anyone else but a Canadian should be in control.

I am an English Canadian and proud of the fact, but I do not think that nationality should enter into the question. I think the soundest approach is the practical approach. I do not care where we get the first governor of the Bank of Canada so long as he knows his business. I would like to know where civilization would have been were it not for a good Frenchman by the name of Pasteur. I have kicked around this world quite a bit. I remember a Scotchman who was chief of a dockyard in Singapore out in the East Indies. If I recall correctly, on one or two previous occasions the late Sir Henry Thornton was criticized because he was a naturalized British subject. He was brought from Great Britain to this country because it was considered that he was one of the greatest railroad men in the world, and I believe the former Liberal government was absolutely sound in that appointment no matter what opinions there may be to the contrary.
I would like to point out to the committee that one of the directors of the Bank of England at the moment is a good Canadian by the name of Peacock, and the people of this country should be proud of him. I am not unmindful of the possibility that there may be an effort by the Bank of England to dominate this country financially, but that problem lies squarely upon the doorstep of the Canadian people and we should not permit any such thing to happen. In our approach to this problem on the basis of high policy, might I say, we should get the best man procurable, and if it is necessary to go to Great Britain, let us go there just the same as wre did in connection with the Canadian National Railways.
I have heard in debates in this house criticisms of the national railways of this country, but I think it has been one of the fundamental driving forces that has placed Canada in the position in which it is to-day. I am not inclined to agree with those who say that we have overbuilt in the matter of railways.

If you read the history of the situation of European countries to-day, you will find that the fact that they are infinitely worse off than we are has been brought about largely by lack of transportation. I make that observation because I think we should approach this problem on a high plane, having in mind the fact that the bank is being established and if it is necessary to go to England for the first governor I do not see any objection to doing so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I feel I must make one or two observations. In the first place I did not say to-day that a Canadian would not be appointed governor; I said that there was no Canadian among the bankers of Canada at present qualified to be appointed governor, and I was so informed by the bankers themselves. It does not follow from that that a Canadian will not be appointed and will so acquire knowledge to carry on the functions of his office. It is unfortunate that we should be asked to accept an amendment which would prevent the appointment to that position of a man like Mr. Peacock, assuming that he would be available, a man who went from 'Canada, trained in London, became a director of the Bank of England, and yet under the amendment moved by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymond) could not be appointed. In the same way nobody else who had been born in Canada and gone elsewhere to acquire his training would be available. This would be the same as saying that you cannot take as president of a university of this country any person other than someone who lives here, the same as saying that your doctor, the man you consult with respect to your own physical condition, must necessarily be a Canadian and nothing else.
Perhaps I have as high an opinion of Canadians as have most men, and I know as much of their attainments and qualifications. When I made the observations I did this afternoon I made them in the light of exact knowledge of qualifications and attainments of members of the banking fraternity who would be available for the position. I endeavoured to make it clear to the committee it well might be that a Canadian might be appointed if he had sufficient time to acquire the necessary knowledge and information to discharge the duties of governor of this bank, but in any event he would have to be assisted by someone who had knowledge.
It seems to me that it is not an edifying spectacle in dealing with a situation of this kind to have the suggestion that we should by law enact that men of the type I mention

Bank of Canada
should not be available for the position and that willy-nilly, fit or unfit, failure or success, we should take for this position men whose residence in Canada would be the sole determining factor if they were good bankers although they knew nothing of central banks. In other words, you do not consult a doctor when you desire to be advised on a question of law, and you do not consult a lawyer when you desire to improve your physical condition. When it is necessary to appoint someone for the purpose of discharging the duties of governor I can only assure the committee that the appointment will be a man who will be well able to discharge those functions, and he must necessarily have knowledge in the first instance. It is no good talking about technical assistance and advice, because there must be under those circumstances one with knowledge with the deputy governor and the assistant deputy governor to enable the business of the bank to be carried on. Every sentence that has been uttered here during the last few minutes magnifying the importance of the office is at the same time a striking illustration of the necessity of having the best man possible available.
I mentioned in the committee what has been reported to have been said by the late J. P. Morgan when he came back from Europe when it was suggested that New York should become the money centre of the world. He said that first of all it was necessary for them to get the men to do the job. They speak of the Bank of England and the advice given to it. Who is one of its advisers? A distinguished American who advised the United States on the matter of the federal reserve bank and things of that kind. There were English and French advisers.
Advice- we agree with that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You cannot advise a man who knows nothing of a matter; he has first to learn something of the rudiments of central banking. You do not appoint a doctor to the bench; you appoint a lawyer; you do not appoint to the position of professor of physiology an eminent lawyer. Banking is a special branch of human endeavour; it is disposed of very simply under two heads. First, we have the commercial banker and, second, the man who has knowledge of central banking. That knowledge can be derived only from countries where there are central banks. I resent very bitterly the observation made in the house that this bank is being created to be an adjunct to the Bank of England. Why is that statement made? There is not the slightest 74726-264
evidence upon which to found it. Why do they say it? Why is that statement being made in this country? Show me a shred of evidence upon which to found it? Why did the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), a former mayor of Montreal, say in this chamber that this bank is to be a branch of the Bank of England? What is the purpose of saying that without a shred of evidence? Why did he say it? I ask him why he said it. The country wants to know why he said it. Why do other hon. gentlemen say it? Why did the hon. member for Vancouver Centre say it?
Because these two gentlemen travelled on the commission.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is, the fact that these two gentlemen were members of a commission appointed to study the banking situation in this country and to assist in digesting the evidence taken, is evidence that this bank is to be a branch of the Bank of England. Imagine a member of the legal profession saying that. When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was asked by the Rockefeller Institute to go to the United States to advise in certain matters, was there any question about that?
We heard about it many times.
During the election they played politics with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That might well be, and it is quite obvious then why this is now being said with respect to this other matter. After Lord Macmillan returned to the old country a dinner was given to him by the Canada Club. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre said, in Canada House; it was not in Canada House. That is mistake number one. Secondly he said that the speeches made at that dinner indicated that this bank was subject to the domination of the Bank of England.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister said I was asked to advise by the Rockefeller Institute; it was the Rockefeller Foundation, not the institute.
Another mistake.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, as long as it was something that bore the name Rockefeller that is sufficient. I corrected that statement only for the purpose of directing attention to the fact that on the return of the chairman of that commission a dinner was tendered to him by the members of the Canada Club, the

Bank of Canada

oldest of the Canadian clubs in England, and the speeches there, as reported in the London Times, did not indicate that there was any suggestion on the part of anyone that there was domination of the situation by the Bank of England. And Mr. Fisher and Mr. Kershaw, to whom reference has been made, were men not sent by the Bank of England but men whom Sir Charles Addis and Lord Macmillan asked to accompany them to act as digesters of the evidence. That is all. There was no secret about it; I saw them here. They were present at the final dinner given to Lord Macmillan by myself. I asked other hon. gentlemen to be present and they were there; they know the speeches that were made on that occasion. I say to this committee that I regard it as a terrible thing to think that this country cannot put on the statute book provision for a central bank without having members rise in this house and say that it is intended to be an adjunct to the Bank of England. Is that an economic argument or just a political argument? Is it intended to serve any useful purpose or to create prejudice? Does it advance anything, does it serve any purpose except to create prejudice in the minds of the people, to say that this bank is to be a branch of the Bank of England?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister, when throughout the general election he spoke continuously of Canada first, was he appealing to prejudice or to patriotism?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The answer is very
simple; he acted upon what he spoke. What is more, the report of the speech made by the right hon. gentleman in Barrie, Ontario, when for the sake of appealing to the few descendants of British settlers in that community he said that Mr. Bennett was talking Canada first, was that calculated to advance the relation between communities?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Half a dozen times that misstatement has been corrected in this house and yet it is repeated. Why does the Prime Minister continue to thresh old straw?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But I say I do stand for Canada first, on all occasions. And what is more, in the centre of the empire I made my position clear. About that there need be no uncertainty, because I believe I can best serve the British Empire by serving that dominion of it in which I live, namely Canada. I believe that is the best way it can be done. I said this afternoon, and I repeat it, that I left with the then Prime Minister a memorandum saying that I be-
lieved that Sir Henry Thornton was eminently well qualified to be the head of our Canadian railways. Without hesitancy I say that. I had just returned from London and I left that memorandum with the then Prime Minister. That does not in any sense indicate that I have not full confidence in Canadians. That is not a question of internationalism, it is a question of countries requiring the services of men specially qualified. Canadian lawyers have made great places for themselves on the bench in other countries. Men from Great Britain have attained to high places in the banking world, and we are now told that these men should not be selected for any position here because they do not live here.
Now the distinction between directors and governors is so simple that it does not require much discussion. The directors, from the very nature of things, have to be Canadians, for this is a Canadian bank. I continue to point out that section 6 is essential for this bank to function. I desire in the most unequivocal terms to say that no relation, direct or indirect, understood or otherwise, by implication or in any other way, between the Bank of England and the proposed Bank of Canada, is possible. The Bank of England is a great central bank and it discharges great functions with all the banks of the world. It will have to do business with the Dominion of Canada, but there is no question of suzerainty, no question of subordination, no question of control. I just want to ask this committee one question: Having heard the ex-mayor of Montreal (Mr. Rinfret) say he was opposed to a central bank and that if I asked the opinion of those who were bankers in Montreal I would not proceed with the establishment of a central bank, is he unmindful of the fact that his own party was committed to that policy? The difficulty is that he cannot understand any party preparing a bill and submitting it to this parliament that involves just what is involved in this bill for the good of the Canadian people regardless of what the great financial interests of this country may say. That is the real difficulty. All you have to do is to read the first few pages of the book by Kisch and Elkin to find exactly why this afternoon I put it to this committee that a government controlled bank does involve political intrigue, as they point out, and one of them at least is regarded as one of the most outstanding authorities in the world on the subject. Such influences lead to chaos and disaster. That is the way he puts it. We have seen an example in this house since three o'clock of what would happen if this had been a publicly owned bank.

Possibly I may be allowed to reply right away to what the Prime Minister has said; as the right hon. gentleman made reference to me, I think it is only proper that I should reply.
I will say in the first place that the very heat displayed by the Prime Minister shows that he at last realizes the importance of the question raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymond), because I have noticed from past performances that the less secure the Prime Minister feels about some attitude or measure the more likely he is to try to drown us under the waters of his indignation. When he points to me and wants to put questions to me because I took the stand in this house-I did it very briefly-that we might perhaps have a Canadian governor for a Canadian bank, and thinks he is going to embarrass me by having me explain to the country why I feel that way, well, my reply is that when we get to the country-and we would like to go there very soon-he will have to explain much more than I shall about this very measure.
I did say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not feel very strongly myself in favour of a central bank, and that in Montreal quite a proportion of the people feel the same way. But my right hon. friend did not understand my argument properly. He said he was following the advice of bankers in not appointing a Canadian governor of this bank.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I made no such statement.

The great embarrassment, in replying to the Prime Minister, is that we can never stop him at a certain point. I appeal to the committee if the Prime Minister did not state that on the advice of bankers he was aware that there was no Canadian able to fill this position, and my retort was that if he followed the advice of certain bankers he would not have this bill at all. That was all. There is no reason to get up in the air because of that; it is a well known fact.
My right hon. friend seemed to be under the impression that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and myself were the only ones to have any suspicion that this bank might be regarded as we suggested. Let me tell him that in Montreal it is current rumour on St. James and Notre Dame streets that this bank is intended to be an adjunct of the Bank of England. I am not speaking for myself; I am saying that this is the
Bank of Canada

common opinion expressed on the streets of the city of Montreal. I want to be kind to the Prime Minister, because I have a very high regard for him. The best way to dispel that suspicion which exists not only in the minds of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and myself but also in the minds of a great number of people in this country, would be to appoint a Canadian governor. If my right hon. friend will do that he will wipe out that suspicion. I am not raising any prejudice; I am being kind enough to bring that prejudice to the attention of the Prime Minister. I am giving him a chance to make good before this bill is adopted. Really I think the Prime Minister is ungrateful for the very kind advice we are giving him to-night.

As a native-born Canadian and I assure the committee it was an accident as far as I was concerned-I think it is very poor statesmanship to take up the time of the committee with a question of this kind. This afternoon we were discussing whether the central bank should be owned nationally or privately, and the question came to a vote. One of the arguments against public ownership and control was that politics might enter into it. I do not hold with that argument, but I believe those who brought it forward could exhibit this discussion as proof that the argument was good.
What is the purpose of the national bank? I think the intention is to use it to improve the economic life of this country. Then if by importing, if you like, a governor and a deputy governor from somewhere else, we can do the job better than we can do it ourselves -I am not saying that would be necessary- for goodness sake let us leave it open to the government to take advantage of that opportunity if it does become necessary. We want the very best administrator it is possible to get; if we have to get that administrator from somewhere else, let us bring him here to help us out. Many of us have gone to Rochester and consulted the Mayo Brothers when we were ill. Surely if we have done that we should not protest against getting the best advice possible in a matter of this kind. My only fear is that the bank may be used for the further exploitation of the people of Canada, as the private banks are used already, and if I am going to be exploited I am not particular whether the exploiter lives in Montreal or in London, England. From the evidence that has been given before the price spreads committee I notice that they can exploit the people in Montreal and Quebec as well as they can in London.

Arts and sciences are international, and to-day the science of banking is as exact as many of the other sciences. We should get the best and most efficient management possible regardless of where it comes from. The only thing on which we should be definite is that when these people come here they should be our servants and do what we tell them to do.

It is to be regretted that on a matter of this importance and after practically the whole house has committed itself to the principle of this bill, a tone of passion should be introduced in dealing with this particular section. I suppose one must remember that we are very close to various provincial elections that have raised passions and the temper of parliament, and perhaps this debate is a forerunner of future speeches to be made in the federal arena. Being altogether disinterested, however, I venture to express an opinion entirely foreign to party considerations and, may I add, to racial considerations as well. I will deal immediately with the argument advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis), which to a certain extent coincided with the argument of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), that we should look first and exclusively to the matter of competence, and that national considerations should not be considered.
If that is the case, Mr. Chairman, why limit this to British subjects? If we substitute imperial nationalism for Canadian nationalism I do not see that we have reached our objective, because we may find in the United States, in Germany, in Italy or in Japan a man more competent to organize a central bank than any British subject at our disposal. If we confine it to British subjects it is because we consider that from a British point of view we should exclude the foreigner. But in order to maintain this institution in its proper character, as an intermediary between Canada and Great Britain and between Canada and the United States in financial matters, I think it is highly important that the directing head should be a Canadian. So far as technical advice is concerned I agree with the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). No one would blame the government for looking for the best experts to be found. I would go this length with the Prime Minister, that probably he would find in the Bank of England or the Bank of France, or perhaps even in the United States, some experts already familiar with the technical business with which this bank will have to deal.

Bank of Canada
But there is another aspect of the question. This bank will have practically supreme control over the economic activities of Canada. If it is important that the head of such an institution should be familiar with affairs in England or the United States or elsewhere, it is at least equally important that the same head should be very familiar with the affairs of Canada and should know the situation of the various classes in Canada. What is the present economic situation of agriculture, of industry, of trade in Canada? What are the present needs of the various classes of producers in Canada, in their dealings with the foreign world? I think the first duty of the governing body of this institution will be, in the very words of the Prime Minister,-words which I applauded when he uttered them and which in my heart to-day I still applaud-* that the first duty of this governor and his board of directors will be to think of Canada first.
I can quite imagine, and it is even plausible, that if you borrow a gentleman from the Bank of England who has the traditional competency and sense of honour that those great English bankers have, most likely he would endeavour to consider his first duty was to Canada. But human nature is there. It has been well said that all the men who have been in the employ of such institutions as the Bank of England or, in the old days, the Hudson's Bay Company, or, in France, the Bank of France, are so imbued with the spirit and traditions of those great institutions that if they go out and serve other institutions they transport with them the spirit of the Bank of England or the spirit of the Bank of France. That is a well known fact, and it is to the great honour of those institutions, that they have instilled such a spirit in the minds and habits of their servants. But I repeat, from our Canadian point of view, in order to establish a proper kind of relationship either with the Bank of England or with the great financial institutions of the United States, is it best for us-is it even best for Great Britain'-that an Englishman should be appointed governor to stand at the head of this Canadian institution? I do not think it is. I repeat, I do not think it is. I think that by force of influence, even with the most honest intention on his part to consider himself, at least for the time being, a servant of Canada, instinctively he would continue to have at heart the interests of the country he left, his country of origin, and of the great institution in that country of which he may have been a servant. Because if we
want to borrow the most competent men in England we must take them from where they have acquired that competency for the managing of a central bank, and that means from the Bank of England.
To show that this was not out of the mind of Lord Macmillan and his English associates I shall point out one part of the Macmillan report. In the appendix to the report, in which there is drafted a skeleton of what the central bank should be, there is a short paragraph which struck me at once, innocent as I am of all technical knowledge in those matters, as a very dangerous one. Paragraph 13 stated:
The hank should maintain a proportion of twenty-five per cenit in gold and foreign exchange against its outstanding note issue and sight liabilities.
It immediately struck me that if the bill to be introduced by the government contained such a disposition with regard to the reserve, it would have enabled our central bank to export the whole of our gold either to London or to New York in exchange for foreign values. Everybody knows that the great struggle in the last fifteen years,-during the war first, but especially in the last fifteen years-has been between the Bank of England, the Bank of I ranee and the Federal Reserve bank of the United states to control gold, to exchange for gold foreign issues or the issues of their own countries in order to accumulate as much gold as possible and thereby to dominate the financial situation of the world. Under a clause such as the one I have quoted, a board of directors, under the direction of an English governor, may well have been tempted, and perhaps for excellent reasons from the governor's point of view, to export the whole of our gold to London in order to strengthen the hand of the Bank of England and the British government, because in national matters the Bank of England and the British government mean the same thing. Although it is not officially a state owned bank, yet, with its old traditions of patriotism, and of service to the state, the Bank of England is as much, and perhaps more, a national institution than would be, in a country like this, a bank with a board of directors chosen by the government. ;So far as that is concerned, I do not know how I would have voted, but I think I shohld have been inclined to vote with the government against the appointment of directors by the government.
It will be the governor and the deputy governor who will rule this institution; let there be no mistake about that. The directors will be the advisers and will probably give
Bank of Canada

a small portion of their time, but they will be devoted to other enterprises. The governor and the deputy governor will be the soul and body of this institution. Therefore, under those circumstances, I insist on what I have said, and I do not speak from a narrow nationalistic viewpoint which, in matters of this kind, should be set aside. The world is suffering too much from extreme and narrow nationalism. I might say that I for one, who for years and years have preached nationalism, have renounced it. I have not renounced the basic principles of nationalism, but I deprecate the practice of nationalism as it is propounded to-day in almost every country in the world. But, as between an extreme and narrow nationalism and the abandonment of all safeguards in the interests of the nation, of its economic life, of its policy,-because, unfortunately in these days economics dominate policy-we should not lay down the principle, first, that Canada is not capable of producing men to put at the head of an institution like this, and secondly that we have to go outside of this country but remain within the circle of the empire to find men to rule an institution which will have to deal-I hope always in friendship and amity-with the Bank of England or with the financial institutions of the other portions of the empire.
We know history and we know human nature. Occasions may present themselves whereby it may become the duty of this institution to resist the influence of the Bank of England, and perhaps to come to terms-I will not say an alliance-but to terms of understanding with other foreign institutions in order to resist the domination of the Bank of England, just as the Prime Minister himself and just as some of his predecessors, including Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to name only two of them, at times had to refer to outside influences to counteract the influence of the British government which wanted to impose upon them certain tenets of policies or certain measures of practical administration, especially in dealings with the foreign world. The so-called civilized world is dying from the fact that questions of money, questions of trade and questions of industry are at the forefront. The so-called civilized humanity and Christianity have forgotten all the great principles which should govern national as well as international relations. But taking facts as they are, we must at the present time acknowledge the predominating influence of money, of national and international trade, of relations between consumers and producers, of balance of trade between countries. If by a closer under-

standing with Great Britain and the other British dominions we can better the financial and economic conditions of this country, and help them to better their own conditions, well and good. But surely it is not by putting a Canadian at the head of this institution that we could endanger our good relations with Great Britain. I agreed with the Prime Minister when he stated in London that he stood for Canada first. I do not say I agreed with the concrete proposals he put before the English people; but with the pronouncement he made at that time I fully agreed, and I applauded him as I applauded when his illustrious predecessor Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the same statement. I applauded him as I applauded his more immediate predecessor, Mr. Meighen, when on the question of the Japanese treaty he told the English government that he would not. consent to a renewal of that treaty because it would be against the interests of Canada. It is the duty of every prime minister of Canada to stand for Canada first, as against England, against France or any other foreign country, provided he does not do that in a narrow spirit of selfish nationalism.
We are now creating the most important instrument in our economic life. We are endeavouring to centralize the forces of money and to bring our private banks under such discipline as will make them serve the interests of the country in preference to the interests of their shareholders or clients. Now that we are endeavouring-I do not say in a perfect way-to give some form of cohesion to our economic life, are we going to lay down the principle that the positions at the head of this most important part of our administrative machinery and organization are to be excluded to Canadians because a few bankers have stated that they do not think there is a Canadian competent enough? I do not ask the Prime Minister to betray any secrets, but it may be that the suggestion arose from the fact that the majority of the bankers do not want to see one of themselves at the head of this institution, because he would know too much about their trade. Perhaps that had something to do with the suggestion made. I believe that if all the directorships of all the private banks of Canada were abolished, many of those bankers would find themselves quite competent to direct the only bank that would remain. I do believe that this was the thought in the minds of the banking advisers of the Prime Minister; but I do not think he should give way to that advice.
As far as the technical advice is concerned, he is quite right. He would receive the

Bank of Canada
approval of every true Canadian if he secured the best possible expert advice, either from England or elsewhere. If on that account he were attacked by French Canadians for not giving them enough positions in the bank, or by Ontario, British Columbia or any other section of the country, I should be the first to defend him. This is probably one of the reasons why the Prime Minister refused to make this a politically governed body. Let this board, with the approval and help of the government, import or invite from England -preferably from England because of the similarity between that country and Canada- or from elsewhere, the best advice obtainable. From a Canadian point of view, from a broad British point of view, from a sensible point of view in the interests of the Canadian people, I cannot agree with the idea expressed by the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Maclnnis) that this is similar to a consultation of the Rockefeller Institute by a sick man who wants advice. Neither do I think that the Prime Minister was true to himself when he quoted a portion of Mr. Taschereau's speech. Mr. Taschereau is an extremely clever man. I think the two ablest men we have in Canada at the present time, even with all their defects, are the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premier of Quebec. I really believe that, but should they begin to take arguments from one another, then I would distrust them. I would be in great disquietude about Canada if that were to happen. It is a good thing that they are opposed to one another.
We have Frenchmen, we have Germans, we have Norwegians in the public service of Canada. In the Department of the Secretary of State it has been necessary to employ foreigners in connection with naturalization matters; but would the Prime Minister appoint a foreigner or an Englishman in Doctor Skelton's place? Would the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) appoint an English lawyer in the place of his deputy? No, they would not, because in matters of this nature, apart altogether from a man's ability, he must know the real conditions of the country in which he lives and for which he exercises his powers. The responsibility of the governor and the deputy governor of this bank will be to Canada, and they should know first the conditions which prevail in Canada. They should have a sufficient knowledge of financial conditions the world over; they should take the best advice possible to obtain, but their main responsibility is to the Canadian people.

propose * to subsection 2. As it stands, this subsection reads:
The first governor, deputy governor _ and assistant deputy governor shall be appointed and their salaries shall be fixed by the governor in council and thereafter appointments shall be made by the directors with the approval of the governor in council.

Monetary policy should be independent of political contingencies and the surest way to

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What statement is that?

The statement that we must beware of sudden fluctuations in political thought in regard to legislation that is now being imposed upon the people of Canada. That is what I resent. It seems to me that we are drifting a long way from democracy when one parliament cannot change the opinion of another when public opinion decides that it has lost confidence in the particular party as it did in 1930. In that case did we attempt to perpetuate our opinions? We did not. Hon. gentlemen opposite have had the opportunity and not only in this but in many instances they are seeking to fasten upon Canada the opinions they possess without any chance of the elected representatives of the people being in a position to change those opinions. That is what I object to and I object to the statement of the Prime Minister in regard to this particular clause as I have objected in many other cases. Surely the people of Canada are entitled by their voice, by their votes, to change any legislation which in their opinion is not in their best interest. To say that because you happen to be in power and possess a majority you are going to perpetuate for at least seven years or until such time as another chamber will have changed its complexion in conformity with public opinion-
You should have abolished the Senate while you were in.

In my opinion when the public do have an opportunity to deal with them they will speak with no uncertain voice.

The bill as it stands now certainly leaves every possibility of a deadlock between the government and the authorities of the central bank if there should be a difference of opinion in regard to the monetary policy to be followed. It seems to me that this amendment is simply to safeguard the

On section 9-Provisional directors.

I want to propose an
amendment to this section, which provides for the appointment of the board of directors. I think in view of what was said this afternoon by some hon. gentlemen that it should be understood clearly that any statement to the effect that as the bill stands, this is to be a publicly controlled bank is not strictly in accordance with the facts. This bank, as this act stands at present, is not publicly controlled. There have been repeated statements n the press to that effect; some such statements have been made in this chamber this afternoon. Under this act every dollar's worth of shares of this bank may be owned by individuals in Canada. Its directors are ten in number, seven of whom, according to section 9 to which we are now directing our attention, are appointed by the shareholders, the people who get together $5,000,000 with which to buy shares and who have no public responsibility of any kind or description. The remainder of the board is made up of the governor, the deputy governor and the deputy minister of finance. The governor in the first instance is appointed by the governor in council, and after the expiration of his first term is appointed by the directors subject only to the approval of the governor in council. The deputy governor in the first instance is appointed by the governor in council, and after the expiration of his first term is ap-
pointed by the directors subject to the approval of the governor in council. The tenth director is the deputy minister of finance, who is entitled to attend the meetings of the board but not to vote. Let me say that the provision with regard to the deputy minister of finance was moved in committee by those of us on this side of the house who felt that there was no attempt whatever by the government to have any supervision over the actions of the board of directors. It now appears as subsection 2 of section 5. To summarize: Seven directors are to be appointed by the' shareholders; two are to be appointed or subject to the approval of the governor in council,, and the tenth is to be the deputy minister of finance, who has no vote at all. The amendment I am now proposing is a considerable' modification of that provision, and in view of the fact that the committee have refused the amendment providing for government ownership this amendment is designed to endeavour to do the next best thing, and ensure governmental or public control. The-provision is an exceedingly modest one, but it is along the line of central bank charters in other countries, to some of which the Prime Minister referred this afternoon. In effect the amendment proposes that four of the seven directors may be elected by the shareholders but that three of the directors must be appointed by the governor in council. These three, along with the governor and deputy governor, who in the first instance are appointed by the governor in council and who after that time are subject to the approval of the governor in council, thereby form a majority of the board. Under the hmend-ment as proposed the seven directors are appointed for what I might call staggered terms; that is to say, so many are retired each year and so many appointed in their place. This provides for continuity of administration and it also provides against the possibility of one government or one party perpetuating the board. This is a sincere endeavour to provide that, along with the directors appointed by the private interests-there shall be a public interest majority in the directors' room. As I have said, Mr. Chairman, this is only proposed as the next best thing to government ownership.
This afternoon, in making the references he did, the Prime Minister seemed entirely to miss the point as to the importance of the functions of this institution which is being constituted by this bill. He seemed to think of this as some sort of little department of government which was being established; or, less than that, some sort of private institution,

Bank oj Canada
something which would carry on business for the purpose of profit. In his remarks my right hon. friend indicated that it was exceedingly difficult for a government to make appointments. Therefore, forsooth, because it was difficult and disagreeable, and because my right hon. friend or whoever occupied that position had to take into consideration certain matters which are always constant in Canada and which exist in connection with any public appointments made by any government anywhere, my right hon. friend asked to be rid of the responsibility entirely.
I do not think the house has ever listened to a more complete abdication of the job of prime minister and of governing this country than this house listened to this afternoon from the right hon. gentleman. He might just as well have suggested that because it is difficult to appoint postmasters, deputy postmaster generals, superintendents of post offices and so on, therefore we ought to hand over the post offices to private shareholders, let them run the post office department and let us just take a share of the profits. He might as well have suggested that the Department of National Revenue be farmed out to some board or some private individuals who would subscribe for stock; that they be given the power to tax, that this country receive a certain percentage of the receipts and that the remainder should go to the private institution. Why? Because it is difficult to make appointments and because one has to consider so many things in connection with making appointments to the public service. That is nothing new; it has existed since the day sixty or seventy years ago when Joe Howe said, "Take away patronage and I will stay in power for fifty years." There always will be difficulties in making public appointments, but that does not excuse my right hon. friend in the slightest for declining the responsibility which I submit is his and the responsibility which rests on this government to see to it that the currency and credit system of this country is preserved under the control of the people of this country, and administered by the government.
Some members of the committee suggested a little while ago that the board of directors has not much power anyway. As my right hon. friend quite properly apprehended, and as he said in answer to that hon. gentleman, the board of directors has more power than perhaps hon. gentlemen think. It is true that the governor and the deputy governor, with one director, form the executive, but it is also true that 'the executive submits its actions to the board of directors. Further than that
it is true that under the act itself there are many important powers vested in the board, and hon. gentlemen must remember that as section 9 of the act stands at present seven of the nine directors who are to perform the functions to which I shall refer are appointed or elected by the private shareholders. The board of directors appoints the governor, the deputy governor and the chairman of the board, subject to the approval of the governor in council. In other words the governor in council is powerless to appoint a governor or deputy governor, after the first appointment, without having such appointments initiated by the board of directors. That is a rather important power to invest in private shareholders. In the second place the board of directors, and nobody else-not the governor-initiates the increase of capital. In other words, unless parliament changes this provision, there can be no increase in capital without first the action of the board of directors. In the third place, and perhaps the most important, the suspension of the twenty-five per cent gold backing, which is laid down here as the basis for the note issue of this central bank of Canada-the initiation of the suspension of that requirement for that ratio is left with the board of directors of the central bank, seven of whom are selected, as the Prime Minister is pleased to portray, by private interests, who are not influenced by racial prejudice, sectional differences, the colour of a man's hair, or anything of that kind-seven men nominated by people who have no other interest in this bank than the fact that they are getting four and one-half per cent. They are the ones who elect the seven out of the nine on the board who will decide as to the ratio of gold backing for note issue of the Bank of Canada, which may go up to over $400,000,000. They are the ones who make that decision, or at least who initiate that decision. Nothing can be done by the governor in council or by the minister until that decision has been first made by the board of directors.
Further than that, they initiate the extension of the suspension. They may initiate an extension of suspension of that ratio to extend for a period of one year, and without their initiation there can be no such suspension. Further than that-and this also is most important-when the question comes up as to what amount shall be paid to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada they are the ones who decide what provision is to be made for all debts, what provision is to be made for depreciation. They are the ones to decide what is left for the purpose of paying over to the consolidated revenue fund,

or to put to rest. Those are the rather important functions of the board of directors, and the amendment which I propose is to provide that a majority of that board shall be at least under the control of or subject to the approval of the governor in council.
What are the functions of the bank? The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) went over them this afternoon as they appear in the preamble to the bill. But the functions are these-and they are set out not only in the preamble to the bill but in the report of the royal commission. They are to provide for the maintenance of national sovereignty over credit and currency. Paragraph 206 of the Macmillan report is as follows:
In the first place, from a national point of view, the central bank, within the limits imposed by law and by its capacities, should endeavour to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation and should so far as possible control and defend the external value of the national monetary unit. In the second place, from the international point of view, the central bank by wise and timely cooperation with similar institutions in other countries, should seek, so far as may lie within the scope of monetary action, to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of economic activity. ...
Then, paragraph 207-and imagine giving this power to a board of directors seven out of nine of whom are appointed by private shareholders:
A central bank is at the same time an instrument and a force. As an instrument it is the means by which the state-which must necessarily retain ultimate sovereignty in matters affecting the currency-can give effect to the national policy. ...
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister and whoever drafted this legislation, and, with all due deference, some of the commissioners who made the suggestions which appear as a schedule, have for a moment forgotten that after all this is a state function, that the control of credit and currency is the biggest and most important public utility in the economic activities of the Dominion of Canada. I am not one who necessarily champions public ownership at all times and in all places, but I say there are certain things which should be under public ownership, or public control and certainly the very first and most important of those is the institution which controls, which guides and which directs the whole economic life of the dominion.
The function with regard to credit and currency is exercised, as has been said repeatedly, by making advances under the section of the bill which provides that this bank may make advances to banks by way of loans, is entitled to purchase securities, and, to a large extent,

the quantity of credit available in Canada, ought to, if this bank is properly regulated and properly run, depend on the rediscount rate and operation of the bank. That is the first method of controlling credit. The second way in which it is done is by open market operation whereby the bank may go out into the market and purchase securities, if it is found that it is necessary, in order to regulate the market, to control the price of money, or to go through the reverse process, and sell them. Those things require people who are first imbued with the point of view of the state, with the point of view of the national interest, with the point of view of public service, and not the control of seven out of nine men who are simply elected as ordinary directors by private shareholders. That board of directors must act as the trustees for the nation, and they are by no means a board of directors in the ordinary sense of the term.
And then we come to the other function, which is just as important, and perhaps more important-and I know the Prime Minister is particularly cognizant of this-the function of endeavouring to maintain the value of our currency internationally, the function of seeing how our gold and currency holdings shall be regulated-because after all, these are the most important things if we are going to have exchange stabilization, and heaven knows that this country needs exchange stabilization in view of our hoped for export trade. I say those things are vital and I say that this power should not be vested in a board of directors seven out of nine of whom are elected by private shareholders.
