These are rather important countries who have felt that government control wholly or by a majority was desirable on their boards. And this brings me to the Dominion of New Zealand, which was the last country to adopt a central bank, and whose legislation has at least to some extent been copied in the bill before us to-night. Let me ask my right hon. friend to bear in mind that New Zealand has exactly the system of control which I propose here. New Zealand has privately owned shares, but New Zealand at the same time has a majority of government control on the board. In New Zealand there is a governor and a deputy governor appointed by the state on the recommendation of the board. There are four directors appointed by the shareholders, two to be actually engaged in farming and two in industrial or commercial pursuits; another three are appointed by the state, and the secretary of the treasury is a member of the board without voting power. As the Prime Minister has said to-day, it would be worth while for us to consider the experience of other countries. New Zealand is well known to be a country which studies economics pretty carefully. New Zealand has gone into the matter thoroughly and has come to the conclusion that government control is the proper thing. I think we would be well advised, outside of the arguments I have endeavoured to put forward, in following the example of New Zealand.
Let me come back again to the argument of my right hon. friend with regard to political control. He heard an address delivered the other day by the Right Hon. Stanley Bruce. We enjoyed his hospitality although he was not present in person. An address was delivered by the Right Hon. Stanley Bruce in connection with the Commonwealth bank of Australia and the work which had been done there. That bank is owned by the people and there is no suggestion of political interference of any kind. The governor stood up to his work and I think it is largely due to his efforts that Australia now finds herself in the situation of being on the right side of
economic recovery. That is what a government controlled bank did. No doubt the government of Australia feared the same difficulties which the right hon. gentleman fears and apprehends in connection with appointments, but that institution has carried on successfully. After all, I think these are largely imaginary lions in the path. The right hon. gentleman has never had very much difficulty in making appointments when he had to make them. We did not approve of them all but he has always taken the responsibility for them and I think he should be quite prepared to again take responsibility. While it may have appeared to be frankness on the part of the right hern, gentleman to discuss this matter of control, let me say here that I challenge him and I challenge any hon. member to find a single case, either in a Liberal or a Conservative administration, where the treasury board of Canada, which has practically as much power as this central bank will have, has shown the slightest evidence of partisan or political control or has been influenced by political considerations in administering the Finance Act. There has been no suggestion of that kind; party politics have played no part.
I submit to my right hon. friend that he might well accept the amendment which I suggest. As I said a minute ago, it is a very modest approach towards what I think there should be in this country, a government owned bank. If we cannot have a government owned bank, let us have government control in the way I have suggested. I submit that it is vital in the interests of this country that the monetary financial and currency systems should be under such control. This bank will have $117,000,000 worth of gold when it is revalued and it will be able to authorize the issue of $468,000,000 in currency. I submit that that is too much power to give to a little group of men who are to be elected by the citizens all over the Dominion of Canada who are able to scrape together $5,000,000, with which to purchase shares in this bank. I submit that this is abrogating the sovereign rights of this dominion and it is practically flying in the face of the principles laid down in the Macmillan report, the recommendations of which we are trying to follow here. I repeat that this is a public utility of the greatest magnitude and importance, and the citizens of Canada should not relinquish control of its administration to any group of private citizens.

Under those circumstances, looking through the volume of Kisch and Elkin that deals with central banks, I find no statute in any country that gives such complete and absolute control, as distinguished from ownership, of any central bank as this one does-complete and absolute, regarding which there can be not the slightest doubt.
The hon. gentleman said I treated this transaction as one of a little state department dealing with a few dollars. Well, I make no boast, but I think I know as much about this central bank bill as any member of this committee; and, what is more, I say that, 74726-265
but for the determination of this government, the pressure from sources indicated by the hon. member for St. James, the ex-Mayor of Montreal (Mr. Rinfret), and from other parts of this country, would have seen to it that there was no central bank that was a real central bank. And when he suggests, as he did, that I do not know what this bill means or contains, I am perfectly content that he should make the suggestion that I was trying to treat this as a little picayune side-wind of the government.
My right hon. friend will find no such expressions of any kind or description. As usual, he is setting up a straw man to knock him down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not suggest that he used those words, but he said this afternoon that he was amazed at the way the Prime Minister had treated the measure, that he had regarded it apparently as some little branch of government and not a great institution that will deal with all these important matters that so greatly concern the country. Well, I am always willing to learn, but I have nothing to learn from that quarter with respect to this bill. I have given more time and attention to this matter than the hon. gentleman has done, great though his attention to it has been. But, as I said a moment ago. both the government and I are deeply grateful that section 14 is there in the terms in which it is, for I could indicate to him the discussion and the efforts to place the question of public control beyond peradventure, to maintain the principle of all great countries whose experience indicates private ownership and public control. I ask any member of this committee who has studied the matter to point to any country in the world in which public control is so absolute in terms, so clear in ensuring the application of the principle of the people controlling the institution.
I will not trespass longer upon the time of the committee because the arguments were answered by the Minister of Finance in the committee. At times one wonders whether or not any good purpose is served by discussions that take three months in committee. All these suggestions have been made, all these amendments we have had this afternoon have been considered

that is, in terms, not in detail-and conclusions arrived at by recorded votes which appear in the minutes of the committee. I will therefore do no more than point out, as I have done, that the supreme power, so far as it is possible to have supreme power and free it from political con-

Bank oj Canada

trol, is vested in the governor in council; and the dangers and difficulties which were pointed out by others, all those peculiar difficulties, we have endeavoured to escape in the manner I have indicated, following the principles laid down by various countries in dealing with the situation.
New Zealand, it is true, has established a central bank. When I was in London at the economic conference last year I gave much attention to this central bank question and discussed it with representatives of the various countries. New Zealand was then discussing the establishment of a central bank, and they were good enough to show us the statute they proposed to enact, and told us of the difficulties they had to encounter. Now New Zealand has launched its bank. It has a capital of half a million pounds divided into shares of five pounds each, and control of the bank with regard to directors is as the hon. gentleman has indicated. The first governor has in point of fact been named and the bank has begun to function. The islands of New Zealand, with a population which is either more or less, I am not sure, than that of the island of Montreal, are dealing with problems that are somewhat different from ours, though there is some essential likeness between the two. And as regards Australia, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman has for the moment forgotten the acute difficulties between the bank and the government with respect to currency matters. Does he realize that it was not the directors of the bank that did it but the governor, Gibson, who made possible the achievement of the supremacy of the governor over the forces that were against him? Now, adjustments, compromises and readjustments have taken place in connection with that matter. The bank came into being as a public bank, owned by the state.
A commercial bank.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, under a Labour government, for the purpose of competing with the chartered banks as it did and as, to some extent, it still does in certain branches of its activities. It became a central bank at a later date, but there was no change of ownership, naturally, by reason of that fact. They have been extremely fortunate in connection with the appointment of governors, and those who have read its history, or heard it as a matter of fact from the distinguished former Prime Minister of Australia, who was here the other day, know something of the difficulties which * they experienced and the way in which those difficulties were overcome. Those who know

all this will realize the importance that attaches to the office of governor.
If I have learned anything from the discussions that I have had and the inquiries I have made, it is as to the desirability of clothing the governor of the bank with the widest possible power. There must always be somewhere some authority who speaks with absolute certainty on problems connected with central banks, and the governor is that person. The governor, in the very nature of things, is clothed with authority not customary in the case of any chairman or any executive officer. For instance, none of our chartered banks, in the persons of their presidents, exercise any such authority or power as may be exercised by the governor of the bank. It is well known that the presidents of our chartered institutions could not for a single moment be permitted to have conferred upon them the power that rests with the governor of the bank. It is related that during his lifetime the late Mr. Harriman secured that the by-laws of the Union Pacific were in such terms that all powers not required by law to be exercised by the shareholders should be exercised by the directors and all powers not required by law to be exercised by the directors in meeting were to be exercised by the president-and he was president. Something of that character may be said about the governor of this bank, the governors of all central banks. All the powers that the shareholders have in general meeting are practically conferred upon the directors, and all powers that the directors have are in terms, unless by law required, vested in the executive committee.
We have further the provision in clause 14 that notwithstanding all the actions that may be taken by the board of directors, all the resolutions they may pass, all the conclusions at which they may arrive, they have no possible effect unless they are approved by the government. I would therefore submit that to the extent of my reading there is no other bank in which you find wider powers of public control conferred, absolute control by governor in council, than there is in this particular case.
There is only one further observation I think I should make. The hon. gentleman said that the Finance Act had practically all the powers of a central bank. I am certain he did not mean that; I am certain no one knows better than he how contrary to experience and fact that is. It was indicated, I think in evidence, that under the Finance Act what happened is that the treasury board once or twice a year, usually once a year, authorizes

Bank o/ Canada
the extent to which borrowings under that act may be made by chartered banks and determines the values to be placed upon securities deposited for the purpose of securing that credit. The maximum of the line of credit was, so to speak, indicated in respect of each bank. I remember reading in the house in answer to a question the line of credit the various banks could secure under the provisions of the Finance Act by reason of a minute of the treasury board fixing that amount and the values to be placed upon the securities lodged for the purpose of enabling currency to be obtained. I hardly think the hon. gentleman would suggest that that is at all comparable with the powers of a central bank
He says that there was never any political interference. In the nature of things the way in which this power was exercised brought about the very conditions that necessitated a central bank. I wonder whether the hon. gentleman has studied closely the operations of the Finance Act. In the light of the experience of this country from the time that act first came into being as an emergency measure to the present time there is just this outstanding fact: there never was in a time of great speculation when there was an enormous volume of currency in this country any effort on the part of the treasury board, because it did not deal with that side of the matter, to control credit and stop speculation. All you have to do is to look at the borrowings and the relation of the Finance Act to the circulation of the country to realize the necessity of a central bank, and I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman said that the rate of rediscount becomes of tremendous importance. When the Bank of England and the Bank of France ran their discount rate up to as high as eight per cent, this was to try to put the brakes on speculation, and I am using the word in a broad sense. The Finance Act and the operations of it under the treasury board were never in the world used for the purpose of endeavouring to deal with that phase of the situation. I speak now subject to correction, but I think if the minutes of the treasury board are looked at, it will be found that not more than twice, and usually once a year from 1915 to date, there was nothing more than an authorization of credit and of the values at which securities were to be taken for the purpose of securing the credit when the applications were made.
This afternoon I was looking at a list in the appendix to the Macmillan report showing the extent to which those borrowings 74726-265J
went. It is amazing to learn what happened, for instance, at the time Great Britain went off the gold standard. At this point I should like to correct a statement attributed to me the other day that I said that this country was not off the gold standard long after it was and I would not admit it was. I say to the committee that this country went off the gold standard on the day following the day that the late Mr. Robb sent $40,000,OOG in gold to New York. I was in opposition at the time and because of certain complications I asked my colleagues in the opposition to say nothing of the matter because I thought to do so might have an injurious effect upon the country. We were off the gold standard from that time, but our gold coverage for our currency never changed since the statute was not amended. We maintained the statute in its integrity until I proposed to make certain amendments to it the other day.
Let me go a step further. Shortly after England went off the gold standard in September, 1931, I met the bankers; I was then in the Finance department and I reduced the rate to three per cent in order if possible to expand credit and meet the difficulties of a situation which then existed.
We were never off the gold standard so far as metallic coverage for our currency is concerned; we were off it only for the export of gold.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. There was no free market for gold, as the books put it, and there was no coverage from that standpoint, but so far as metallic coverage for currency is concerned there was never a change.
The effect of that reduction may or may not have been beneficial; I ana not expressing any opinion on that point, but the reduction in the price paid for the accommodation received under the Finance Act was for the purpose of meeting that situation. In October the high level of borrowing under the Finance Act was $24,500,000; the low being $9,000,000. In November the high level was $66,500,000, the low being S17,500,000. That indicates quite clearly that while there was an expansion or contraction of credit there was no supervision by the treasury board of that contraction or expansion. They never purported or undertook to do so; there was nobody there for that purpose. Anyone who knows the circumstances knows the chairman of the treasury board was the Minister of Finance, and there never was any effort made to deal with those problems of expansion and contraction of credit and all the questions allied to the credit problem to which the hon. gentleman referred that must be
Bank of Canada

dealt with by an efficient central bank. I do not think he intended to convey what his words, literally taken, would mean, that is, that the powers under a central bank were those which might be found in the provisions of the Finance Act. That is too far-reaching a statement to make, because there was no supervision and no control at any time with respect to matters of that kind.
We believe that by the methods we have adapted we have met the situation, and clause 14, which the hon. gentleman is entitled to credit for having suggested in the committee, concerns a matter which has given considerable thought to those responsible for the legislation. It has been said to-day that somebody must take the responsibility for it. This government takes the responsibility for this legislation. When we went into the committee we explained that as regards any constructive suggestions that might be made, if we could reconcile them to our view of what we were seeking to do we would gladly accept them. The rapidity with which the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman was embodied in clause 14 is an indication that the government wanted a supervision of that character, but we knew if we undertook to insert it when the bill was prepared what condemnation we would have received for having done so.
That is a very high plane.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the fact with respect to this legislation. I do not look upon this as being legislation regarding which a government must have views for the purpose of enforcing them-not at all. I have never in all my little experience with legislation approached any problem with a greater sense of individual responsibility, and I have never endeavoured to obtain information from so many sources to enable me to arrive at sound conclusions. If I have arrived at conclusions which are at variance with those of my hon. friends opposite I trust they will credit me with sincerity in my convictions, as I do them, except when they endeavour to interject politics into it. I think this far transcends purely political views. Every action that has been taken in connection with this measure has been first of all to maintain the sense of a great public trust on the part of the shareholders, to relieve this bank from any possible interference with its operations through political intrigue, to use the language of the volume to which I have already referred; secondly to ensure that there shall be continuity of policy by having one of the permanent members of the civil service, the

deputy minister of finance, a permanent member of the board, so that there shall be continuous knowledge on the part of the minister, and that means' the government of the day, of the operations of the bank. And thirdly, to ensure that the governor of the bank, who is responsible for its operation in the large true sense of the term, should be one who represents the government of the day. He is appointed in the first instance by the government, and there can be no appointment made thereafter that is not acceptable to the government. And no resolution or action of the board of directors of any kind, shape or form, or of the executive committee, can become effective unless the governor approves. Therefore I submit frankly, and as fully as I can from the knowledge that I possess, what little it may be, that there is no central bank to which reference can be made in a country such as this, with conditions as they are, where public control has been so clearly defined and can be easily exercised as in this bill, and at the same time maintaining what Kiseh and Elkin think should be maintained, the sense of private ownership of shares, vesting in those who have them the sense of a great public trust.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question? If the government parts with both public ownership and public control of a great financial institution such as the Bank of Canada will be, is there not a possibility that at a time of crisis a situation might arise in which the power of this bank will be greater than that of the government itself? Might not the bank be in a position to defy the government if it so desired? I use the word "government" rather than the word "parliament" because I know the Prime Minister will say that parliament can always alter any law that has been made. But I am assuming a moment of crisis at some time of financial stress in the affairs of the country or of the world when this bank would be operating. The government has parted with ownership of the bank; it has parted with the control of the bank. It has a limited control but not the final control. Both the ownership and the control will be in private hands. This will be the great banking power of the nation. Under those circumstances is there not a possibility, assuming the government may wish to act in such an emergency, of a situation arising where the government would be less powerful in dealing with it than the corporation which it has created?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, if the right hon. gentleman has read the history

Bank of Canada
of what recently took place in Australia, he will have observed there was a moment when the attitude of the government was at variance with that taken by the governor of the bank. Had the view of the government prevailed in that particular instance I think it is now generally conceded that the results would have been ruinous. The fact that the governor of the bank was a man of such firmness of character and determination that he carried out the plans that were made they believe was largely responsible for the success following the efforts that were made for rehabilitation at a time when the situation became acute.
To admit that there is a possibility of differences of opinion between the government and the governor of the bank is but to admit that there is always the possibility of differences of opinion. That I think may be taken for granted. That is, there might be a moment when the view of the governor of the bank and that of the Minister of Finance of the country might be at variance. That might happen. But I cannot conceive of that happening as a practical question, because with the continuous communication betwen the government and the bank, the government of the day doing what it thought desirable as conditions changed from time to time, the governor of the bank, with his wide knowledge of international conditions, his wide experience in the bank and knowledge of conditions in his own country, I should say would be perfectly willing to accommodate his views to those of the government if no question such as aroce in Australia was to be considered. In Australia at one time the question involved the movement of the gold itself. It will be recalled that substantially the gold reserve was moved to Great Britain, if my memory serves me, and deposited in the branch of the bank there, to save the credit of the commonwealth at that particular moment. I speak subject to correction. Then subsequently the differences of opinion were adjusted; the governor did succeed in having his views prevail, with the result that Australia emerged from the situation. But that was a case in which it was thought at the time that the government took a rather extreme view, because of the attitude of some people with respect to certain qee-tions of interest and other matters of that character, involving, I should say- although perhaps Australians would not like me *e u-e the word-possible repudiation. Perhaps if I put it that way I am fair to the right hon. gentleman. I do not conceive that in this country, as I know it. that need give us such concern as would necessitate any
change being made in the proposals submitted to the committee. If I did I would say so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to enlarge a little on what I have in mind. In the world of finance the money power, as it is termed, is of course the all important factor, a factor that many people believe is greater than the power of government itself. What I am anxious to be perfectly sure of is that the government of the day, in parting with some of the ownership of money power, as it is doing, and so completely with the control that it has of money power, to a privately owned and controlled institution which will be allied to all of the banks of the country and through them to all the financial interests of the country, is not bringing about a situation in which at some critical time should a question arise as between the financial interests in a large way and the interests of the public as represented by the government in a large way, the two might clash, and the government find itself powerless, at least until parliament could be called together, to deal with the situation. In the meantime in such a case the financial interests may have had their way in the furthering of their ora interests, albeit their action might be against the public interest. I do not say they will act that way; I am quite prepared to believe that those who may be appointed will be honourable men and will seek to do what as they see it is the right thing. But with affairs as they are in the world to-day the point of view of those who think that a certain thing is right may differ very much, depending upon whether it is to the financial end of things they are looking, or to social and public ends.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, and I think that
what the right hon. gentleman has said is dealt with by Kisch and Elkin in the volume to which the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred, commencing at chapter 2. There is recognition of the very fact to which the right hon. gentleman has referred, namely the power of the money interest, and it is for that reason that the conclusion seems to have been arrived at that it is safer to have the central bank a privately owned and government controlled organization than otherwise. I will not take time to read more than this:
The tendency of the nineteenth century, particularly as regards actual statutory provisions. was somewhat to stress the control of the state over the central bank. The case of the Reiehsbank may be cited as an instance of a general disposition to regard a state or semistate bank as analogous to a state railway
Bank of Canada

system or a state tobacco monopoly. The war period exhibited in extreme terms the danger of this system. Since then the tide has set strongly against granting the state power to interfere with the functioning of a central bank.
Then follow statements about it, and the writer continues:
Central banks have more and more come to be looked upon as analogous to large public trusts and' less and less as departments of state.
Then he goes on to discuss the matter with respect to many central banks. At page 18 he says:
The case for the direct intrusion of the state into the actual workings of a nicely balanced economic machine loses its force as soon as the public responsibilities and public objects of the institution are fully recognized by those responsible for its management and in the code of legal provisions or established tradition by which they are guided.
Then he inserts this paragraph:
Thus in times of crisis the bank, like many other normally independent organizations, is likely to find itself to a large extent under the influence of the government. At all other times, however, its independence is secure and unassailed. The inner history of the Bank of England is known only to those in authority, but it is probably safe to assume that the relations of that institution with the government present few difficulties that are not capable of amicable solution. The bank has in the course of years built up a body of tradition and experience directed to the public service which is unrivalled, and it may be fairly surmised that no government in this country would seriously attempt to intervene in its administration.
Then he refers to the German bank, the opening sentence of its charter being:
The Reiehsbank is a bank independent of government control.
We have gone much further than that. The discussion that follows, at pages 22 and 23, with respect to banks might be worth looking at, without taking up too much time:
As long as convertibility is maintained the worst evils resulting from government intervention in banking and currency control are avoided. Doubtless the governments which have laboriously dragged themselves out of the morass of inflation will not readily slip back; nevertheless, if the control of the operations of the central bank lies directly or indirectly with the government, it becomes fatally easy for the government to finance itself for a time by means of book entries and short loans from the bank, a course which is the first step towards currency depreciation and inconvertibility.
Even apart from such risks there are other serious dangers from a government controlled bank. The network of financial and commercial life is so intricate, and the decisions of the bank on important points have such widespread results, that all interests are not
TMr Bennett.1
affected in the same way. A change in the rate of discount, for example, which benefits some may be unwelcome to others. But if the government has a controlling influence over the bank, there are obvious ways by which the more powerful interests in the country can try to enforce their wishes. The road is open for political intrigue, and there can be no safeguard that the policy of the bank will be carried on without bias as national interests require. It seems a paradox that when the object is to secure the execution of a national policy, this should not most readily be achieved by the creation of a state bank under official control; but even in the countries where the capital of the bank is held by the state, steps have been taken in certain instances to remove its administration from political influences and to give it a measure of independence from the government.
I will not take time to quote more than those observations. I really do not think there is any more danger here than there is with respect to the relations of the Bank of England with the government of that country. That is an old institution, with established traditions. It will take many years for us to establish like traditions, but I believe that can be done more effectively and efficiently by the means provided in the bill, particularly- I say again-section 14, which in its present form we owe to the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). I believed something of that sort was essential in this bill, and I say again I think that is one of the most powerful of the provisions of the bill to ensure the efficiency and effectiveness of government control as against government ownership.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is one other question I should like to ask the Prime Minister. Is there not a danger, if the government parts with both ownership and control of the central bank, of some government being seriously embarrassed in the matter of carrying out its trade and fiscal policies? Let me instance what I have in mind. Assume that private interests in control of the central bank are favourable to a policy of trade within the empire; let us say, are in favour of promoting trade within the empire to the exclusion if need be of trade by Canada with other countries throughout the world. Is it not possible, through the control of credit which this central banking institution will possess, that its officers may be in a position to cause their policy to be made to prevail rather than that the government should be in a position to have its policies prevail? It seems to me that unless the government has some control or some ownership of this central institution there will be that danger at all times. Where you have an administration whose policies as to trade

Bank of Canada
harmonize with the policies of the bank as to finance; assume for example, that both have imperial policies in trade and finance, there everything might work very smoothly. But assume that the bank once established is determined on certain imperial policies, and it is likely to have such as a guiding principle if the governor of the bank is to be chosen from the old country and assume that the government of the day should seek to promote world trade even if such a policy should happen to some extent to be at the expense of trade within the empire itself, is there not a danger of this institution being in a position to make it very difficult, if not impossible, for the government, representing the people, in its policies to carry out those policies as effectively as it otherwise would be able to do?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am bound to say, Mr. Chairman, that the very organization of this bank in this form is calculated to prevent that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In what way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will try to explain. If
the government were in complete control of the bank it would mean that if you had one government succeeded by another the bank would naturally change its policy, assuming that the policy was as the right hon. gentleman suggested. Then you would have governments controlling policies without continuity. What we wish to secure is a policy based upon the economic conditions of the country, not a policy of the bank based upon policies of a government. That is what the right hon. gentleman desires.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have always felt that the government represented parliament. If a government or a political party has placed certain policies before the people and the people have endorsed those policies, returning the party to power in order to enforce them, it seems to me that no institution should be created by the state which could interfere with the will of the people as thus expressed through their representatives in parliament. It is that danger that I confess I see in this institution as it is to be constituted under this measure. That, just as the Prime Minister says, you may have the bankers desiring continuity in their banking policy, and determined to have it even if it runs counter to what may be the trade policy or the fiscal policy of the government of the day. You will almost certainly, sooner or later, have a conflict between financial and fiscal policies, the former in the control of private interests the latter in the control of
the government. If there is a conflict anywhere my feeling is that the view that ought to prevail is the view of the administration of the day, not the view of any institution privately owned and controlled that may originally have been given power by the state.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Of course the only difficulty about that is the fact that it is always so difficult to say that a particular policy has been approved by the people. That is always the difficulty where you have no direct referendum upon a particular matter. That is why that on the continent of Europe they contend so vigorously for the submission of questions in order that there may be a direct determination by the people. I need not remind the hon. gentleman, with his wider knowledge than mine, of what that has led to, but that is a fact. There can be no policy of the central bank, as related to the chartered banks and the country, that is not similar to all. The deputy minister of finance is familiar with the transactions of the central bank and its relation to the chartered banks. The chartered banks continue to establish credit for the industrialists and the agriculturists, just as they do now. The only difference is that the central bank supplies the requested credit to the individual chartered banks to carry on, where formerly under the provisions of the Finance Act reliance was placed upon that measure.
Let us assume that the government of the day is apprehensive of the continued evidence of speculation on the part of the people, and it has made up its mind that something must be done to curb their activity. The government discusses the matter, and the Minister of Finance says to the deputy minister, "You may indicate to your board and to the bank the desirability of raising the discount rate for the purpose of enabling that to be done." The Minister of Finance sends for the governor, and discusses the matter with him. It is common, of course, in countries like France and continental Europe, for the minister of finance to be constantly in communication with the governor of the bank. He says, "We must raise the discount rate." The discount rate is raised from four per cent to six per cent. Still the speculation continues on the stock exchanges, and last year the rate was raised to seven per cent. I think, if my memory serves me correctly, that it went as high as eight per cent at one time.
Did that stop speculation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It had a very great effect upon it, yes. And it will be recalled that the central reserve bank of the United States made
Bank oj Canada

some effort in that direction. It is also within the memory- of this committee and those who have read the report of the Macmillan commission that in the opinion of Sir Charles Addis there is no central bank in the United States. I fancy, as a matter of fact, there is not any central bank of the United States. There are, of course, twelve central reserve areas or regions in which there are what I think they call regional banks. The member banks are the banks within that region, and the control of the government is as was indicated by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth. But there is no eon-tral bank dealing with the question of credit and rediscount rates in the manner in which we have been dealing with those matters.
I will say this to the right hon. gentleman: if between now and to-morrow any thought that may be given to this measure by hon. members opposite would result in indicating wherein they see the possibility of that danger, I shall endeavour by appropriate terms to remove it. But I see no likelihood of there being any such exercise of that power. I did look into something which was said in this house on a former occasion, and as the bill stands I cannot see that it would be possible for that result to follow. If there is any member of the committee who has any suggestion to make which would indicate that that is a possibility, I should certainly be very glad to have it, and the government would welcome any suggestion in that direction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to make clearer what I have in mind. In a word it is this: Taking matters as they are at present, it seems to me that so far as this House of Commons is concerned, as respects the banking and financial institutions of the country, it makes very little difference what particular trade policy we may have. We feel an absolute security in our ability to give effect to our own trade policy. But under this measure the government is parting with some measure of ownership-what in this bank will become privately owned. It is parting to a certain extent with the control it now has over the regulation of credit. It is not merely creating an institution which will be privately owned and controlled, but it is parting with a certain control by government which it has to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In what way?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This bank will have the issue of currency and it will have the control of credit, which at least to some extent, through the Department of Finance, the government itself is able to exercise to-

The powers which the government there had are now being transferred to this privately owned institution. If you alter the situation by taking away from the government the power that it has to-day; and the banks are lo be allowed to control the central bank-for that is what it really amounts to, the banking interests are all to be one, the central bank being in private hands let us put it that way -there is, it seems to me, a real danger of the financial control which may thus be exercised by the bank being exercised against what may be the fiscal policy of the government of the day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should be glad to give the matter such reasonable attention as I can between now and to-morrow, and if the right hon. gentleman or any other member of the committee sees that danger, and indicates to me where it is to be found in the bill. I shall certainly consider it and try to provide a remedy against it, because I realize there is no desire to place the question of the fiscal policies of governments in the hands of the banks of the country, either the central bank or any other bank. I cannot conceive that it is possible under this measure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The line of
remedy will lie in the matter of control; the government ought certainly to have a very large measure of control over this institution, I would say " the " control of the institution. The question of ownership, is, I think debatable.
Progress reported.
